Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession1/46
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • CFA Institute: the global body that runs the CFA Program and sets its Code of Ethics.
  • Member and candidate: a CFA Institute member, or someone enrolled in the CFA Program. Sharma ji is a charterholder, Chintu a Level I candidate, Pinky neither.
  • Client: a person or institution whose money or interests a professional looks after.
  • Compliance: the in-house team that checks staff follow laws and firm rules.
  • Conflict of interest: when what is good for you or your firm is not good for the person you serve.
  • Cost of capital: the return investors demand before they invest.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession2/46
Story

Sharma ji's one-word interview question

Chintu's first week at a Mumbai investment firm. He is a CFA Level I candidate. Sharma ji, the CIO and a CFA charterholder, asks him to define ethics. Chintu tries a joke. Sharma ji does not laugh.

Ethics is a set of moral principles and rules of conduct that guide behaviour: what is good or bad, right or wrong, and what we ought to do. Ethical conduct is behaviour that follows those principles and balances your own interest against the effects of your actions on other people, direct and indirect.

Not getting caught measures luck, not ethics.

Ethics is about what you ought to do, especially when your interest and someone else's pull in different directions.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession3/46
Building blocks

Ethical principles: the beliefs under the rules

Ethical principles are beliefs about what is good and acceptable behaviour. Families, religions and cultures word them differently, but in finance the same few keep returning: honesty, fairness, diligence (doing the work properly), respect for the rights of others, loyalty and transparency.

A principle does not tell you exactly what to do on a Tuesday afternoon. It tells you what to weigh. When two principles clash (loyalty to a friend versus honesty to a client), you need judgment, and often more specific rules.

Principles are broad beliefs about right conduct; they guide judgment but do not script every action.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession4/46
Know the difference

Code of ethics versus standards of conduct

Code of ethicsStandards of conduct
Whatwritten principles a group commits tominimum behaviours required of members
Detailbroad, the valuesspecific, what you must and must not do
Exampleact with integritydo not act on inside information

The code states what a profession values. Standards turn those values into rules that can be checked, taught and enforced. Most professional bodies have both, and they work together.

Code = the principles; standards of conduct = the minimum specific behaviour that puts the principles into practice.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession5/46
Why bother

Why a profession writes a code at all

A written code does five jobs:

  1. Communicates the group's values to members and to the public.
  2. Guides members in grey areas where the law is silent.
  3. Sets a minimum level of conduct everyone must meet.
  4. Gives a basis to discipline those who break it.
  5. Signals trust: clients can rely on a member without checking everything themselves.

The last job only works if the first four are real.

A code earns trust for a whole profession only when members follow it and someone enforces it.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession6/46
Story

You can squeeze a mango, not a fund manager

At the Crawford Market fruit stall Chintu's mother squeezes a mango and knows if it is ripe. She can judge the product herself.

A client cannot do that with investment advice. The professional knows far more about risk, fees, skill and the products themselves. This gap is called information asymmetry. Results arrive years later and mix skill with luck, so even a bad adviser can look good for a while.

So the client has to trust. Ethics is what makes that trust safe.

Clients cannot easily check the quality of investment services, so the industry runs on trust, and trust needs ethics.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession7/46
Key idea

Fiduciary: holding someone else's money

A fiduciary is someone trusted to act in another person's best interest, usually while controlling their money or decisions. Portfolio managers, trustees and many advisers are in this position.

The client hands over money, information and power. In return the professional owes loyalty (client first), prudence (sensible decisions) and care (doing the work properly).

Whether a role is a legal fiduciary depends on the country and the job. Ethically the direction of the duty is the same: towards the client.

A fiduciary controls someone else's money and must put that person's interests first.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession8/46
Picture it

Trust is the real product

When investors trust professionals and markets, more of them take part. Markets get more liquid, prices become fairer, and companies raise money more cheaply.

When a scandal breaks that trust, investors leave or demand a higher return to compensate for the risk of being cheated. The cost of capital rises for everyone, including honest firms that did nothing wrong.

That is why ethics is not charity. Over the long run it is good business for firms, markets and the whole economy.

Ethical conduct builds trust, which brings in investors and lowers the cost of capital; broken trust does the reverse.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession9/46
Story

The 18% fund that never was

Sunrise Capital, a fictional Pune fund, reported 18% returns every single year, smooth as malai. Rs 100 "grew" to Rs 270 in six years.

In reality it was losing money. New investors' cash paid the old ones: a Ponzi scheme. When new money slowed, it collapsed. Real value: Rs 70 per Rs 100.

Damage: 4,000 families lost savings. Staff lost jobs. The regulator tightened rules for every fund. Honest managers now face clients asking "are you a Sunrise too?"

Returns that look too smooth to be true usually are.

One fraud harms clients first, then the firm, then every honest firm and the market's reputation.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession10/46
Who gets hurt

One cheat, four victims

WhoHow they are harmed
Clientslose money and stop investing
Firmfines, legal costs, lost clients, damaged brand
Marketsdistorted prices, fewer investors, less liquidity, higher cost of capital
Professionpublic trust falls, regulation and costs rise for everyone

The cheat usually pays too: job, career, fines, sometimes jail. But the bill is shared by many people who never broke a rule.

Unethical behaviour harms clients, the firm, the market and the whole profession, not only the person caught.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession11/46
Story

The front-runner of Dalal Street

Raju, a fictional dealer at a Mumbai broker, sees a pension fund's order to buy 5,00,000 shares of Kesar Foods. Before placing it, he buys the same stock for his wife's account. The big order lifts the price; he sells 15 minutes later.

The pension fund paid about Rs 0.50 more per share: 5,00,000 x 0.50 = Rs 2.5 lakh extra, money taken from retirees.

Other traders bought at a distorted price. The broker was fined and Raju was banned. It looked like "just a small trade".

Front running takes money from clients and distorts prices, so it harms clients and the market at once.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession12/46
Key idea

What makes a profession

A profession is an occupation that serves others using specialised expertise and is trusted to police itself. Common features:

  • Specialised knowledge and skills built through long study.
  • High entry standards: exams, qualifications, experience.
  • A code of ethics and standards of conduct.
  • Monitoring and enforcement: breaking the code has consequences.
  • Commitment to clients' interests above the professional's own.
  • Continuing education to stay competent as knowledge changes.
A profession = expert knowledge + entry standards + a code that is enforced + client first + lifelong learning.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession13/46
Compare

A job versus a profession

JobProfession
First dutyto the employer and the taskto clients and the public, then the employer
Entryset by each employercommon standards and exams
Rulescompany rulesa code enforced by peers, plus company rules
Learningoptionalexpected for life

Doctors and chartered accountants are classic professions. A profession also earns privileges, such as self-regulation, because society trusts it to put clients first.

A profession differs from a job in putting clients first and in having shared entry standards and an enforced code.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession14/46
Apply it

Is investment management a profession?

Run the checklist. Investment management has specialised knowledge (valuation, risk, markets); entry standards such as the CFA Program and regulators' exams for some roles; a code of ethics such as CFA Institute's; enforcement by professional bodies and regulators; a duty to put clients first; and an expectation of continuing education.

The catch: there is no single global licence, and many people in the industry belong to no professional body. So trust has to be earned firm by firm and person by person.

Investment management has the features of a profession, and bodies like CFA Institute exist to strengthen them.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession15/46
Challenge 1

Situational influences: the pull of the moment

Situational influences are outside factors in the moment that shape what we think and do. In finance the usual ones are:

  • Money and prestige: bonuses, promotion, rankings, being seen as a star.
  • Loyalty to the employer or to colleagues.
  • Pressure from bosses or from important clients.
  • The firm's culture: what everyone around you treats as normal.

People tend to underestimate how strongly the situation pushes them and overestimate the role of their own good character.

Situational influences (money, prestige, loyalty, pressure) bend decisions more than people expect.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession16/46
Story

Pinky and the loyal cover-up

Month end. Bunty, a fictional trader on Pinky's desk, marks his bond positions at friendly prices to hide a loss. Clients' statements will show values that are not real. Pinky tells Chintu to stay quiet: "Bunty covered for me last year. Desk loyalty."

Loyalty to colleagues feels like a virtue, and here it is the trap. The people who pay are clients who see false values and the firm that will face the regulator.

Loyalty to colleagues or the employer never means helping them deceive clients. Chintu should take it to his supervisor or compliance.

Loyalty is a powerful situational influence; it never justifies hiding misconduct that harms clients.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession17/46
Story

Pressure from above and from outside

Mehta sir, a fictional head of sales, wants this quarter's fund sales up 30%. A big client, Mr Bajaj, wants his board report to show only the one good quarter. Chintu sits in the middle.

Pressure from bosses and from clients is a classic situational influence. It rarely arrives as "please commit fraud". It arrives as "be a team player" or "keep the client happy".

A fair report shows all periods. Chintu can offer to explain the bad quarters, but he must not hide them.

Pressure from bosses and clients is real but does not change what is right: report fairly and push back.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession18/46
Challenge 2

Overconfidence: "I would never..."

Pinky is sure she is more ethical than her colleagues. Most people are sure of that. It cannot be true for everyone.

Overconfidence bias in ethics means believing "I am a good person, so whatever I decide is ethical." It makes people skip the checks, ignore warning signs, and blame others' lapses on bad character while blaming their own on circumstances.

The fix is humility: assume you can be influenced, slow down, and use a framework or ask someone before a hard decision.

Overconfidence in your own ethics is a danger sign; it stops you from questioning your decisions.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession19/46
Challenge 3

Short-term focus

Quarterly results, monthly fund rankings and annual bonuses reward what happens now. That tempts people to grab short-term gains whose costs come later: pushing unsuitable products, hiding a loss until next quarter, trading too much to earn commissions.

The shortcut looks great on this quarter's chart. Later come complaints, fines, lost clients and a lost career. Ethical choices tend to pay slowly but keep paying, because trust compounds.

A short-term focus hides the long-term costs of unethical choices; good decisions look at consequences over time.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession20/46
Challenge 4

Why good people make bad decisions

Most scandals are not run by cartoon villains. They are run by normal people who took one small step, then another.

  • Small steps: each step feels only a little worse than the last.
  • Framing: it feels like a "business decision", so the ethical side fades from view.
  • Excuses: "everyone does it", "no one is hurt", "I will fix it next month".
  • Situational pressure, overconfidence and a short-term focus push in the same direction.
Bad decisions usually come from small steps, pressure and excuses, not from bad people; spot the first step.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession21/46
Exam trap

Challenges: what the exam checks

  • People underestimate situational influences and overestimate their own character. Answers that say "a good person will always act well" are wrong.
  • Money and prestige, loyalty to employer or colleagues, and pressure from bosses or clients are the named situational influences.
  • Overconfidence and a short-term focus are separate challenges; know which one a case shows.
  • Loyalty to the employer does not mean following an unethical instruction.
  • A culture that only asks "is it legal?" (a compliance-only culture) is weaker than one that asks "is it right?".
When a case blames "pressure", "loyalty" or "the bonus", the answer is a situational influence.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession22/46
Picture it

Legal and ethical are two different circles

Law and ethics overlap a lot, but not completely.

  • Legal and ethical: most daily work. Honest research, fair fees.
  • Legal but unethical: selling a high-fee product the law allows to a retiree who does not understand it.
  • Ethical but illegal: rare; for example, breaking an unjust secrecy law to expose a fraud that is hurting thousands of people.
  • Neither: trading on leaked results in most countries.
Legal does not mean ethical; ethics usually asks for more than the law.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession23/46
Key idea

Why the law is not enough

  • Laws lag practice. New products and tools appear first; rules come years later after something goes wrong. In the gap, only ethics protects clients.
  • Laws differ across countries. What is banned in one market may be allowed next door, and investors cross borders.
  • Laws set a minimum. They describe what society will punish, not the best conduct.
  • Laws have loopholes and can sometimes be unjust.

So professionals cannot outsource their conscience to the rule book.

Law is a slow, local minimum; ethics fills the gaps where law lags, differs or stops short.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession24/46
Sort them

Four cases, four regions

Place each case in a region before you open it.

Answers
  1. Paying for your chai: legal and ethical.
  2. High-fee fund sold to a retiree who does not understand it: often legal, but unethical; it serves the seller, not the client.
  3. Exposing a large fraud by breaking an unjust secrecy law: can be ethical but illegal.
  4. Trading on leaked results: illegal in most countries and unethical everywhere.
Ask two separate questions: is it legal, and is it right? The answers can differ.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession25/46
Exam trap

Ethics versus law: the wording tricks

  • "The action was legal, so it was ethical" is a classic wrong answer.
  • "Laws are the same everywhere" is wrong; they differ across countries.
  • "Laws adapt as fast as markets" is wrong; laws usually lag.
  • Ethical standards are generally higher than legal ones. But a law can be stricter than a code on a specific point, so do not assume the code always demands more.
  • "Ethical but illegal" exists but is rare. Exam answers rarely reward breaking the law.
Treat "legal" and "ethical" as two tests; passing the legal test alone is never enough.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession26/46
The tool

The ethical decision-making framework

When a choice is hard, use four steps:

  1. Identify: the relevant facts, the stakeholders and the duties you owe them, the ethical principles involved, and any conflicts of interest.
  2. Consider: situational influences, alternative actions, additional guidance (policies, codes, laws) and advice from others.
  3. Decide and act.
  4. Reflect: was the outcome what you expected? Why or why not?

It is a loop, not a straight line. New facts send you back to the start.

Identify, consider, decide and act, reflect: learn the order and what goes in each step.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession27/46
Step 1

Identify: facts, people, principles, conflicts

  • Facts: what exactly happened, and what do I not know yet?
  • Stakeholders and duties: who is affected, and what do I owe each one? Clients, employer, colleagues, the market, the profession.
  • Ethical principles: which ones are in play (honesty, fairness, loyalty, independence)?
  • Conflicts of interest: where does my interest, or my firm's, differ from the client's?

Most bad decisions skip this step and jump straight to "what do I want?".

Identify = facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession28/46
Step 2

Consider: pressures, options, guidance, advice

  • Situational influences: is a bonus, a boss, a client or loyalty pushing me? Would I decide the same if nobody were watching or paying?
  • Alternative actions: there are usually more than two. Accept, decline, delay, disclose, escalate.
  • Additional guidance: firm policies, the law, professional codes and standards.
  • Seek advice: compliance, legal, a supervisor or a trusted mentor. Asking is a strength, not a weakness.
Consider = situational influences, alternative actions, additional guidance and advice before you decide.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession29/46
Steps 3 and 4

Decide and act, then reflect

Decide and act: pick the action that best meets your duties after weighing the options, and then actually do it. A good decision that never gets carried out helps nobody.

Reflect: afterwards ask: was the outcome what I expected? Why or why not? What would I do differently? Reflection turns one case into better judgment for the next one, and may show that you need to loop back because new facts have appeared.

Reflect asks whether the outcome matched what you expected, and why; it feeds the next decision.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession30/46
Case 1, part 1

The broker's free Goa trip: identify and consider

Speedy Securities (fictional) invites Chintu on a free four-day Goa trip. Chintu helps choose which brokers get the firm's trades, and clients pay those commissions.

Identify. Facts: valuable gift, from a broker he helps pick. Stakeholders: clients (want the best trade execution at a fair cost), his employer, the broker, Chintu. Principles: independence, loyalty to clients. Conflict: the trip could tilt future trades towards Speedy.

Consider. Influences: it is free, fun, "everyone goes". Options: accept, decline, pay his own way, ask first. Guidance: the firm's gift policy. Advice: compliance.

A gift from someone whose business you control is a conflict of interest, whatever its label.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession31/46
Case 1, part 2

The broker's free Goa trip: decide, act, reflect

Decide and act. Chintu tells his supervisor and compliance about the offer, as the gift policy requires, and declines the trip. If the firm says it may attend a real business event, it pays his travel itself.

Reflect. Two months later Speedy's execution quality slips. Chintu moves the trades to a better broker with no guilty feeling and nothing to explain. Outcome as expected: his judgment stayed independent.

Verdict

Asking first and declining keeps him clean. Quietly accepting a lavish trip from a broker he helps select would put his independence, and the clients' interests, at risk.

When in doubt about a gift: disclose, ask, and let the client's interest decide.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession32/46
Case 2, part 1

"Make it a Hold": identify and consider

Chintu's model says Kesar Foods (fictional) is overpriced: Sell. Mehta sir, a fictional head of sales, says Kesar pays big banking fees: "Make it a Hold."

Identify. Facts: the analysis says Sell; the pressure is commercial, not analytical. Stakeholders: investors who rely on the report, the firm's clients, the firm, Kesar, Chintu. Principles: honesty, independence, objectivity. Conflict: banking fees versus honest research.

Consider. Influences: pressure from a boss, fear for his job. Options: change it, refuse, ask Sharma ji to review the model, go to compliance. Guidance: the firm's research policy.

Pressure to change a rating for business reasons is a conflict between the firm's fees and the readers' interests.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession33/46
Case 2, part 2

"Make it a Hold": decide, act, reflect

Decide and act. Chintu asks Sharma ji to check the model. It holds up. The rating stays Sell, the reasons are documented, and Chintu reports the pressure to compliance. Had the firm forced the change, he should refuse to sign a report he does not believe.

Reflect. Kesar's banking team is annoyed. Compliance adds a rule: sales and banking staff cannot see draft ratings. The outcome was harder than Chintu hoped, but he expected that and still finds it right.

Verdict

Changing the rating to please a banking client would be dishonest to every reader. Keeping the supported rating and escalating is right.

Research must say what the analysis supports; escalate pressure instead of bending to it.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession34/46
Exam trap

Framework: what the exam checks

  • Order: identify, consider, decide and act, reflect.
  • Conflicts of interest, stakeholders and duties owed are found in identify.
  • Situational influences, alternative actions, additional guidance and seeking advice belong to consider.
  • "Was the outcome as I expected, and why or why not?" is reflect.
  • The framework is iterative: new facts send you back. It is not a one-time checklist.
  • It does not hand you one right answer; it helps you reach a better decision and explain it.
Match each item to its step: conflicts in identify, influences and advice in consider, outcome review in reflect.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession35/46
Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. Ethics = moral principles that guide conduct; ethical conduct weighs self-interest against effects on others.
  2. Code = broad principles; standards = specific minimum conduct.
  3. Clients cannot easily judge advice (information asymmetry), so the industry runs on trust.
  4. Unethical acts hurt clients, the firm, markets (higher cost of capital) and the profession.
  5. Profession: expertise, entry standards, enforced code, clients first, lifelong learning.
  6. Challenges: situational influences, overconfidence, short-term focus.
  7. Legal is not ethical: laws lag, differ by country, set only a minimum.
  8. Framework: identify, consider, decide and act, reflect.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the ethics and trust chapter.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession36/46
Exam question 1 of 10

Ethics matters more in investment management than in many other businesses most likely because:

  1. A. clients often cannot easily judge the quality of the service they receive
  2. B. investment returns are guaranteed by regulators once a firm is licensed
  3. C. investment laws are the same in every country
Show answer

Answer: A. A is right: information asymmetry (the professional knows far more, and results mix skill with luck) forces clients to rely on trust. B is wrong: regulators do not guarantee returns. C is wrong: laws differ widely across countries.

Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession37/46
Exam question 2 of 10

Which statement best distinguishes a code of ethics from standards of conduct?

  1. A. A code of ethics is enforced by law; standards of conduct are voluntary.
  2. B. A code of ethics states broad principles; standards of conduct set specific minimum behaviours.
  3. C. A code of ethics applies to firms; standards of conduct apply only to regulators.
Show answer

Answer: B. B is right: the code states values and principles, and standards turn them into specific required conduct. A is wrong: a professional code is enforced by the professional body, not by law, and standards are not voluntary for members. C is wrong: both apply to the members of the group.

Pick an answer before you tap.

Exam question 3 of 10

Which is least likely a common feature of a profession?

  1. A. A code of ethics that is monitored and enforced
  2. B. High standards of entry such as exams
  3. C. A guaranteed minimum income for every practitioner
Show answer

Answer: C. C is right: professions do not guarantee income; it is not a defining feature. A and B are both classic features of a profession, along with specialised knowledge, client focus and continuing education.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 1: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession39/46
Exam question 4 of 10

After a large fund manager is exposed for faking returns, investors across the market demand higher returns before investing. This is most likely an example of how unethical behaviour:

  1. A. raises the cost of capital, including for honest firms
  2. B. harms only the clients of the firm involved
  3. C. improves market efficiency by removing a bad firm
Show answer

Answer: A. A is right: lost trust makes investors demand compensation for the risk of being cheated, so capital costs rise for everyone. B is wrong: the effect here spreads well beyond the firm's own clients. C is wrong: removing one firm does not offset the market-wide damage to trust.

Pick an answer before you tap.

Exam question 5 of 10

Pinky says, "I have never done anything unethical, so I do not need to check my decisions with compliance." Her statement most likely shows:

  1. A. a short-term focus
  2. B. loyalty to colleagues
  3. C. overconfidence in her own ethics
Show answer

Answer: C. C is right: believing that being a good person makes every decision ethical is overconfidence bias. A is wrong: nothing here is about trading future costs for present gains. B is wrong: she is not protecting a colleague.

Exam question 6 of 10

Chintu stays silent about a teammate's misleading client report because the teammate helped him last year. The challenge to ethical behaviour that most likely explains this is:

  1. A. a situational influence
  2. B. information asymmetry
  3. C. a fiduciary duty
Show answer

Answer: A. A is right: loyalty to colleagues is a named situational influence. B is wrong: information asymmetry describes the knowledge gap between professional and client, not Chintu's motive. C is wrong: a fiduciary duty would push him to protect clients, not to stay silent.

Exam question 7 of 10

Which statement about ethics and the law is most accurate?

  1. A. Conduct that is legal is also ethical.
  2. B. Laws often lag behind new market practices and products.
  3. C. Ethical standards never require more than the law.
Show answer

Answer: B. B is right: laws usually arrive after new practices create problems, leaving a gap that only ethics covers. A is wrong: many actions are legal but unethical. C is wrong: ethical standards usually ask for more than the legal minimum.

Pick an answer before you tap.

A fund sells a legal but very high-fee product to elderly clients who clearly do not understand it. The conduct is most likely:

  1. A. legal and ethical
  2. B. ethical but illegal
  3. C. legal but unethical
Show answer

Answer: C. C is right: the law allows the sale, but it serves the seller at the expense of clients who cannot judge it. A is wrong: being legal does not make it ethical. B is wrong: nothing here breaks the law.

A broker offers Chintu, who helps choose the firm's brokers, an expensive free holiday. Using the framework, his most appropriate next action is to:

  1. A. consider the firm's gift policy and seek advice from compliance before deciding
  2. B. accept, because the gift is legal in his country
  3. C. accept, and decide later whether the gift affected his choice of brokers

Answer: A. A is right: in the consider step he weighs additional guidance and seeks advice before acting. B is wrong: legal does not settle whether it is ethical, and his independence is at stake. Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced1/47
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • CFA charterholder: has passed all three exams and met the work rules. Sharma ji is one.
  • Candidate: a person enrolled in the CFA Program, e.g. registered for Level I. Chintu is one.
  • Non-member: no CFA Institute membership or candidacy. Pinky is one.
  • Material nonpublic information: important news about an investment the market does not have yet.
  • Jurisdiction: a country or region whose laws apply to you or your business.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced2/47
Story

Who referees the referees?

Chintu asks Sharma ji who makes the rules for CFA charterholders. "Same people who set your exam," says Sharma ji.

CFA Institute is a global, not-for-profit association of investment professionals. It runs the CFA Program, writes the Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, and enforces them through its Professional Conduct Program. Its stated mission is to lead the profession by promoting the highest standards of ethics, education and professional excellence for the ultimate benefit of society.

It is a professional body, not a government regulator.

CFA Institute writes the Code and Standards and enforces them on its own members and candidates.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced3/47
Key idea

Who must follow the Code and Standards

  • Members of CFA Institute, including CFA charterholders: Sharma ji.
  • Candidates enrolled in the CFA Program, at any level: Chintu, even before he passes anything.
  • Not bound: non-members such as Pinky, and firms. CFA Institute disciplines individuals, not companies.

Pinky still has to obey the law and her firm's rules. CFA Institute just has no power over her. Members and candidates are also encouraged to tell their employer that they are bound by the Code.

The Code and Standards bind CFA Institute members and candidates only, not non-members and not firms.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced4/47
Quick cases

Who is bound? Four people, one rumour

A takeover rumour from a friend inside the target company goes round the office. Who can CFA Institute act against if they trade on it?

Verdict
  1. Sharma ji: yes, he is a member.
  2. Chintu: yes, a candidate is bound from enrolment, not from passing.
  3. Pinky: no. The regulator and her employer can act; CFA Institute cannot.
  4. The firm: no. CFA Institute sanctions people, not companies.

If Chintu helps Pinky trade, Chintu still breaks the Standards.

First question in every ethics case: is this person a member or candidate?
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced5/47
The documents

The rulebook and its user guide

Two documents matter:

  • The Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, in force from 1 January 2024. Short: six Code lines, seven Standards. CFA Institute, Code and Standards
  • The Standards of Practice Handbook, 12th edition (2024). Long: it explains each Standard, gives guidance, recommended procedures for compliance and worked examples.

The exam tests the handbook's interpretation, not your own idea of fairness. If your notes are older than 2024, check the titles below.

Learn the 2024 Code and Standards and read them the way the 12th edition handbook does.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced6/47
What changed

The 2024 update in three lines

Standard2024 change
I(E) Competencenew: have and keep the competence your job needs
V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clientsadds: disclose the nature of the services and their costs to the client
VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflictswas "Disclosure of Conflicts": now avoid a conflict or disclose it; disclosures must be prominent and in plain language

Some web pages and older books still use the old VI(A) title. Same Standard. CFA Institute blog, Jan 2024

2024: I(E) Competence added, V(B) now covers services and costs, VI(A) now says avoid or disclose.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced7/47
Enforcement

The Professional Conduct Program

The Professional Conduct Program is how CFA Institute enforces the Code and Standards. It runs under the CFA Institute Bylaws and its Rules of Procedure, which aim for a fair process: the person is told about the matter and can respond, and investigations are kept confidential.

Professional Conduct staff investigate. A Disciplinary Review Committee of volunteer members hears cases the person disputes and decides sanctions. It is peer review: professionals judging professionals.

Professional Conduct staff investigate; volunteer peers on the Disciplinary Review Committee decide disputed cases.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced8/47
Enforcement

How an inquiry starts: five doors

  1. Self-disclosure: on the annual Professional Conduct Statement, a member or candidate reports a complaint, lawsuit, regulatory action or criminal matter about their professional conduct.
  2. Written complaints from clients, colleagues or anyone else.
  3. Public sources: news reports and regulators' published actions.
  4. Exam proctor reports of conduct in the exam room.
  5. Analysis of exam materials, and monitoring such as social media posts about exam content.
Inquiries start from self-disclosure, complaints, public sources, proctors, or analysis of exam materials.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced9/47
Enforcement

The investigation and its three outcomes

Professional Conduct staff gather facts. They can ask the member or candidate for a written explanation, interview the person, the complainant and other third parties, and collect documents and records.

Then the staff decide:

  1. No disciplinary action is needed.
  2. Issue a cautionary letter: a warning, not a sanction.
  3. Discipline: find a violation and propose a sanction.
After investigating, staff close the case, send a cautionary letter, or propose a sanction.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced10/47
Enforcement

Accept the sanction or ask for a hearing

If staff propose a sanction, the member or candidate chooses:

  • Accept it, and the matter ends with that sanction.
  • Reject it. The case then goes to a hearing panel drawn from the Disciplinary Review Committee, which hears both sides and decides whether there was a violation and what sanction fits.

So no one is sanctioned only on staff's word if they choose to contest it.

A person who rejects a proposed sanction gets a hearing before a panel of Disciplinary Review Committee members.

Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced12/47
Case

Bablu's well-dressed calculator

Bablu, a fictional Level I candidate, slips formula notes inside his calculator cover. The proctor spots them and files a report.

Who: a candidate, so bound. Door: a proctor report. Standard: VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs.

Verdict

Violation. Staff investigate and propose a sanction. Likely outcome: his exam result is voided and he is suspended from the CFA Program for a period. Had he passed the exam without the notes ever being found, it would still be a violation; getting away with it changes nothing.

Exam misconduct by a candidate goes through the same conduct process and can void results and suspend candidacy.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced13/47
Exam trap

Enforcement: what the exam checks

  • A cautionary letter is a warning, not a sanction.
  • CFA Institute is not a regulator: it cannot fine, jail or ban anyone from the industry. Its power is over membership, the designation and the CFA Program.
  • Firms and non-members are outside its reach.
  • A member who disputes a proposed sanction gets a hearing; the case is not closed automatically.
  • Self-disclosure on the annual Professional Conduct Statement is one of the ways an inquiry starts.
  • Candidate sanctions are about the program: suspension, prohibition, voided results.
Enforcement answers turn on three facts: who is bound, what the outcomes are, and what CFA Institute cannot do.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced14/47
The Code

The Code of Ethics in six lines

Members and candidates must:

  1. Act with integrity, competence, diligence and respect, ethically, towards the public, clients, employers, colleagues and other market participants.
  2. Put the profession's integrity and clients' interests above their own.
  3. Use reasonable care and independent professional judgment.
  4. Practise professionally and ethically, and encourage others to.
  5. Promote the integrity and viability of global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.
  6. Maintain and improve their competence, and help others improve theirs.
Six Code lines: integrity, clients first, care and independent judgment, professionalism, healthy markets, competence.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced15/47
Practise it

Which Code line? Four office moments

  1. Sharma ji pays for a course on credit derivatives because his fund now buys them.
  2. Chintu keeps his own rating after a broker hints he should raise it.
  3. A charterholder coaches juniors on how to handle client complaints honestly.
  4. A member refuses to trade back and forth with a friend just to make a stock look busy.
Answers

a: line 6, competence. b: line 3, independent judgment. c: line 4, encourage others to practise ethically (and line 6). d: line 5, integrity of capital markets.

Each Code line has a recognisable everyday form; learn to spot it.

The map

The seven Standards on one page

The Code is six broad principles. The Standards of Professional Conduct turn them into seven groups of specific rules, 23 sub-standards in all:

  1. Professionalism (5)
  2. Integrity of Capital Markets (2)
  3. Duties to Clients (5)
  4. Duties to Employers (3)
  5. Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions (3)
  6. Conflicts of Interest (3)
  7. Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate (2)

Memory hook: Pinky Can't Cheat Every Investor, CFA Rules. CFA Institute

Seven Standards: Professionalism, Capital markets, Clients, Employers, Investment analysis, Conflicts, Responsibilities as member or candidate.

Look-alike titles

Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced25/47
Key rule

Follow the stricter of the law and the Standards

Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law: understand and obey all applicable laws, rules and regulations, including the Code and Standards. Where they conflict, follow the more strict one.

  • Find every law that applies: where you live, where you do business, where the client is.
  • Law stricter than the Standards: follow the law.
  • Standards stricter, or no relevant law: follow the Standards.

The Standards never permit breaking a law, and a law never excuses breaking a stricter Standard.

Always apply the stricter of the applicable law and the Code and Standards, point by point.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced26/47
Worked example

Case A: the local law is stricter

Sharma ji works in Country S, whose law bans fund managers from accepting any gift from brokers. A broker sends a Rs 3,000 pen set. Under the Standards alone, a modest gift that could not reasonably affect his judgment might be acceptable.

  1. Applicable rules: Country S law and the Standards.
  2. Which is stricter on gifts? The law: it bans all of them.
  3. So the law wins on this point.
Sharma ji must return the pen set. Following the Standards does not excuse breaking a stricter local law.
When local law is stricter than the Standards, follow the law.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced27/47
Worked example

Case B: the local law is less strict

Chintu works in Country L, where only company insiders are banned from trading on inside news. Pinky's cousin at Kesar Foods leaks an unannounced takeover; Pinky passes it to Chintu.

  1. Who: Chintu is a candidate, so the Standards apply. Pinky is not.
  2. Country L law: Chintu is not an insider, so trading is legal there.
  3. Standard II(A): anyone with material nonpublic information must not act on it. Stricter.
  4. So the Standard wins.
Chintu must not trade or pass the tip on. Pinky is outside the Standards; whether she can trade depends only on Country L law.
When the Standards are stricter than local law, follow the Standards.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced28/47
Worked example

Case C: where you live versus where you work

Sharma ji lives in Country S (strict law) but runs money for clients in Country L (loose law, looser than the Standards).

  1. If only Country L law governs this business: L is less strict than the Standards, so follow the Standards.
  2. If Country S law also governs him (it applies to its residents wherever they work) and it is stricter than the Standards: follow Country S law.
  3. If neither country has a relevant law: follow the Standards.
Work out which laws actually apply, then follow the strictest of those laws and the Standards. A looser law in the place of business never lowers the bar.
Residence versus place of business only decides which laws apply; the stricter-rule test is the same.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced29/47
Related rule

When others break the law: dissociate

I(A) also says: do not knowingly participate in or assist a violation, and dissociate from it. Staying silent while knowing can count as assisting.

How to dissociate: raise it with your supervisor or compliance first; refuse to work on it; take your name off the report or product; in extreme cases, resign.

The Standards do not require you to report the matter to a government regulator unless the law requires it, though doing so may be wise. Reporting a member's violation to CFA Institute is encouraged, not required.

Faced with a violation, dissociate: escalate internally, refuse to take part, and remove your name.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced30/47
Exam trap

Law and the Standards: the wording tricks

  • "Follow local law because you work there": wrong if the Standards are stricter.
  • "Follow the Standards even though local law is stricter": wrong; the stricter law wins.
  • "Must report the violation to the regulator": not required by the Standards, unless the law requires it.
  • "Must resign immediately": rarely the first step; dissociate first.
  • "The Standards override the law": no, they stack on top of it.
The right answer is nearly always "the stricter of the two", plus dissociation if others are breaking the rule.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced31/47
Exam method

Five questions for any ethics case

  1. Who is it? Member, candidate or neither. Neither means the Standards do not apply to that person.
  2. What duty, to whom? Clients, employer, the market, CFA Institute.
  3. Which Standard? Name the sub-standard, using the look-alike checks.
  4. Is there a violation? Compare what happened with what the Standard requires, not with what feels fair.
  5. What is the most appropriate action? The step the handbook recommends, usually disclose, get consent, escalate or dissociate.
Who, duty, Standard, violation, action: answer all five before reading the options.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced32/47
Exam method

Reading the question stem

  • "Most likely": pick the best fit, even if another option is partly true.
  • "Least likely" or "does not": you are looking for the false statement or the action that complies. Circle the word before reading options.
  • "Most appropriate action": the best of the three; it can be imperfect.
  • "According to the Standards": use the Standards, not local law or the firm's policy.
  • "Required" versus "recommended": recommended procedures are good practice, not rules. Skipping one is not automatically a violation.
Underline the stem's key word (most, least, required, recommended) before you look at the options.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced33/47
Exam trap

Distractor patterns

  • Right verdict, wrong reason: "Violation, because he made a loss." The reason must match a Standard.
  • Extreme action: resign at once, sue, call the regulator. Usually the right first step is to disclose, ask, escalate or dissociate.
  • "It was legal" or "firm policy allows it": not a defence if the Standards are stricter.
  • Non-member "violates": the Standards do not bind them.
  • "Disclosure fixes everything": some conflicts must be avoided, and some things need written consent.
Eliminate options with the wrong reason, the wrong person, or an extreme action; the survivor is usually right.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced34/47
Worked example

Walkthrough 1: a "most likely" question

Pinky (not a member or candidate) tells Chintu (a Level I candidate) about an unannounced takeover of Kesar Foods. Chintu buys 500 shares for himself. Who most likely violated the CFA Standards? A. Pinky only. B. Chintu only. C. Both.

  1. Who: Pinky is neither, so she cannot violate the Standards. Chintu is a candidate.
  2. Duty: to the integrity of the market.
  3. Standard: II(A) Material Nonpublic Information.
  4. Violation: Chintu acted on material nonpublic information. Yes.
B. Chintu only. Pinky may still be breaking the law, but that is not a CFA Standards question.
Check who the person is before judging what they did.
Ch 2: The Code of Ethics, the Standards and How They Are Enforced35/47
Worked example

Walkthrough 2: a "least likely" question

Sharma ji's country allows managers to accept any gift from brokers. Which action is least likely to comply with the Standards?

  1. Who: Sharma ji is a member, so the Standards apply.
  2. Stricter rule: local law allows all gifts, so I(B) Independence and Objectivity is stricter.
  3. A complies: declining is always allowed. B complies: a modest token cannot reasonably sway judgment.
  4. C fails: a luxury holiday could reasonably compromise independence; "it was legal" is not a defence.
C. Least likely means find the action that breaks the Standards.
In a "least likely to comply" question, the answer is the one violation hiding among compliant actions.

Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. Bound: members and candidates. Not bound: non-members, firms.
  2. 2024 Code; handbook 12th edition. New I(E); VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.
  3. Inquiries: self-disclosure, complaints, media, proctors, exam materials.
  4. Outcomes: no action, cautionary letter, or sanction (reject it: hearing).
  5. Members: censure, suspension, revocation. Candidates: suspension, voided results.
  6. Code: integrity, clients first, care, professionalism, markets, competence.
  7. 7 Standards, 23 sub-standards: know titles and who each protects.
  8. Follow the stricter of law and Standards; dissociate from violations.
