Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism1/56
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • Candidate: anyone enrolled in the CFA Program; bound by the Standards from enrolment.
  • Compliance: the team inside a firm that checks staff follow laws and firm rules.
  • Issuer: the company whose shares or bonds are analysed or sold.
  • Sell side, buy side: brokers who publish research; fund managers who buy securities.
  • Investment banking: the bank unit that raises money for companies, for fees.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism2/56
Story

Five temptations before lunch

9:05 am at a Mumbai fund house. Chintu, a Level I candidate, finds five things waiting: a request to skip a compliance check "just this once", a broker's Diwali hamper, a pitch deck promising "guaranteed 18%", a colleague's family dinner filed as client entertainment, and a derivatives mandate nobody on the team understands.

Sharma ji: "Five problems, one Standard. Professionalism. Data dikhao: which part is which?"

Standard I of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct (updated effective 1 January 2024) has five parts: I(A) Knowledge of the Law, I(B) Independence and Objectivity, I(C) Misrepresentation, I(D) Misconduct, I(E) Competence.

Standard I asks five things of a professional: obey the rules, stay unbiased, tell the truth, behave honestly, and be able to do the job.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism3/56
Picture it

Who the Standards bind

The Code and Standards bind CFA Institute members and candidates. A candidate is bound from enrolling in the CFA Program, so Chintu is covered before he passes anything.

Pinky is a trader but neither a member nor a candidate. The Standards do not apply to her. Laws and her firm's rules still do.

Employers are not bound by the Standards, though many adopt the Code. A member answers for his or her own conduct whatever the firm does.

Exam habit: before asking "which Standard?", ask "is this person a member or candidate?"

No member or candidate, no Standards violation, though a legal problem may remain.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism4/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

I(A) Knowledge of the Law, in plain words

Understand and comply with every law, rule and regulation that governs your professional work. That includes governments, regulators, licensing bodies, professional bodies, and the Code and Standards themselves.

  • Where the law and the Code differ, follow the stricter.
  • Do not knowingly take part in or assist any violation.
  • Dissociate from any violation you know about.

You need not be a lawyer. You must know the rules of your own job and ask compliance or legal counsel when unsure.

Know the rules of your job, follow the stricter of law and Code, never knowingly help a breach, and dissociate from one.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism5/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

Stricter rule wins, even across borders

List every rule that governs the activity: your home law, and the law where you do business if that law says it applies to you. Then compare each with the Code and follow the stricter.

SituationFollow
No relevant lawCode
Law weaker than the CodeCode
Law stricter than the CodeLaw
Weak home law, but a stricter client country law applies to youClient country law

Compare issue by issue: a law can be stricter on disclosure while the Code is stricter on gifts.

Find every rule that applies, then obey the strictest one; weak local law is never an excuse.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism6/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

Dissociate: what it means in practice

Dissociating means separating yourself from the wrongdoing. Keeping quiet while carrying on is not enough.

  • Raise it with your supervisor or the compliance department. Confronting the person directly can also help.
  • Refuse to work on the matter: take your name off the report, step off the account or project.
  • Keep a record of what you saw and did.
  • If the violation continues and the firm will not act, resigning may be the only way out.

Inaction plus continued involvement can be read as knowing participation.

Escalate, step away, write it down; resign only if the breach goes on.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism7/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

Whistleblowing: what is required and what is not

TellRequired by the Standards?
Supervisor or complianceThe usual first step of dissociating
Regulator or other authorityNo. It may be appropriate, and some laws require it
CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program (it investigates breaches)No, but strongly encouraged for breaches by members or candidates

Acting against an employer's interests to protect clients or the integrity of the market, and not for personal gain, does not breach the duty of loyalty to the employer.

The Standards require dissociation, not a report to the regulator; the law may require more.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism8/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

I(A) decision flowchart

Use it on any I(A) question:

  1. Which rules govern the activity? Include the Code.
  2. Which is stricter on this issue? Follow that.
  3. Is someone, you included, breaking a rule? If you know it, you must not take part or assist.
  4. Dissociate: escalate, step away, document, and resign only if it continues.

The exam usually asks for the most appropriate first action. That is almost always going to the supervisor or compliance, not the regulator or the exit.

Rules first, stricter rule second, then dissociate from any breach you know about.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism9/56
I(A) Knowledge of the Law

I(A) recommended procedures

WhoWhat to do
Member or candidateStay informed on rules and changes; check the firm's compliance procedures are adequate; keep reference files on applicable laws current; know the rules in each country where you sell; seek compliance or legal advice when unsure; document any dissociation
FirmDevelop or adopt a code of ethics; give staff information on applicable laws; set up procedures for reporting violations
Members keep up and escalate; firms write the code, share the rules and build a reporting channel.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism10/56
I(A) case pair

The juiced-up pitch deck

Case 1. Chintu finds the firm's pitch deck shows returns from before the fund existed as if they were real. He tells Kapoor, the sales head, who shrugs. Chintu keeps emailing the deck to prospects: "Sales owns it."

Verdict 1

Violation of I(A). The deck breaches the Code. He knows it and keeps helping spread it. He had to stop and escalate.

Case 2. Same discovery. Chintu stops sending the deck, writes to compliance with details, asks to be taken off the mailing, and keeps a copy of his note.

Verdict 2

No violation. Dissociation done right. No report to the regulator was required.

Knowing about a breach and continuing to help is participation; stopping, escalating and documenting is the fix.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism11/56
I(A) case pair

No law there, so anything goes?

Case 1. Sharma ji runs a fund from Mumbai for clients in Country Q, which has no rules on disclosing conflicts. A colleague says: "No law there, so no disclosure." Sharma ji discloses the conflicts anyway, as the Code requires.

Verdict 1

No violation. With no stricter law, the Code is the standard to meet.

Case 2. Country R's law lets advisers keep referral fees secret. Ravi, a charterholder there, takes fees for sending clients to a broker and tells no one. The Code requires disclosing referral fees to clients.

Verdict 2

Violation. The Code is stricter, so it governs. Local permission is no defence.

When the Code asks more than the law, the Code wins.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism12/56
Exam trap

I(A) traps

  • "Legal" is not the finish line. If the Code is stricter, legal conduct can still violate I(A).
  • Options saying you must report to the regulator are usually wrong. The Standards do not require it; a specific law might.
  • Resigning is the last step of dissociating, not the first.
  • Silence is not neutral when you keep working on the matter.
  • "Knowingly": unknowingly helping someone else's breach is not participation, but ignorance of your own job's rules is no excuse.
  • Pinky is not a member or candidate. Her breach is a legal problem, not a Standards violation.
Stricter rule, knowing participation, dissociation before resignation, and no duty to report to regulators: the four I(A) pivots.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism13/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

I(B) Independence and Objectivity, in plain words

Use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in your professional work.

Do not offer, solicit or accept any gift, benefit, compensation or consideration that could reasonably be expected to compromise your own or someone else's independence and objectivity.

The test is how it reasonably looks, not whether you felt swayed. Clients need advice driven by facts, not by who paid for lunch.

Giving, asking and taking are all covered; the test is whether it could reasonably compromise judgment.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism14/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Gifts: who is giving changes the rule

FromRiskRule
Client, as thanksLower: rewards past workDisclose to employer, before accepting where possible, otherwise after
Broker, issuer or manager seeking businessHigher: aims at future decisionsOnly modest gifts and entertainment within firm limits

The Standard sets no money limit; firms set one. Sweets at Diwali or a business dinner is usually modest. A family holiday is not. A client bonus tied to future performance needs the employer's written consent under IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements.

Client thank-yous: disclose. Gifts from people who want something: modest or refuse.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism15/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Issuer-paid research

Small companies often pay for research to get noticed. That is allowed, with guardrails:

  • a flat fee, agreed before the work starts;
  • pay not linked to the conclusions or the rating;
  • thorough, independent, unbiased analysis;
  • the report discloses that the issuer paid and the nature of the payment.

A bonus for a Buy rating breaks I(B). So does a fee that grows with the target price.

Issuer-paid research is fine only with a flat, unconditional fee and full disclosure.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism16/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Company visits: who pays for the trip

A company invites analysts to see its new plant. The visit is useful. Who pays is the issue.

  • Best practice: you or your firm pay for commercial travel and hotels.
  • Where commercial transport is not available, such as a remote mine, modestly arranged travel from the company is acceptable.
  • Refuse lavish extras: charter jets where airlines fly, luxury resorts, golf weekends.
Pay your own way where you can; accept only modest help where you cannot.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism17/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Pressure from investment banking

Sell-side firms earn banking fees from issuers. Bankers may want a friendly rating on a deal client. The analyst must publish an honest view anyway.

  • Firms separate research from banking with firewalls, so bankers cannot direct research.
  • Analyst pay should not depend on banking deals.
  • If the firm will not publish negative views on a deal client, it should put the company on a restricted list and publish only factual information, rather than biased research.
A rating reflects the analyst's honest view or it is not published; it is never bent for a banking client.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism18/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Pressure from clients, issuers and your own firm

Buy-side clients: a fund manager holding a stock, perhaps a big commission payer, leans on a sell-side analyst not to downgrade it.

Issuers: a company threatens to cut an analyst out of calls and meetings after a negative report.

Your own firm: a portfolio manager whose performance depends on a holding pushes in-house analysts to stay positive.

Same answer every time: listen to anyone, but let no one write your rating.

Pressure from clients, companies or colleagues never changes the analysis.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism19/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Choosing managers and custodians

Fund manager and custodial relationships: members who hire and keep outside managers, custodians (banks that hold clients' securities) or other service providers must not accept gifts, entertainment or travel that could be seen as swaying the choice. A fund-of-funds manager wined and dined by a manager seeking money is the classic case.

Manager selection: both sides are covered. The hiring side, such as pension staff or consultants, must not solicit favours. The side pitching for the mandate must not offer anything that could reasonably sway the decision.

When a mandate or a custody contract is being chosen, nobody on either side trades favours.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism20/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

Credit rating agencies

Credit rating agencies grade the default risk of bonds, and are usually paid by the issuers they rate. That creates pressure to rate generously.

  • Members working at an agency should make sure procedures stop the issuer influencing the analysis, and follow their agency's and the industry's conduct rules on analysis and report distribution.
  • Members who use ratings should know about the conflict and consider whether an independent credit assessment is needed, instead of relying on the rating alone.
The issuer-pays model is a built-in conflict: raters guard their process, users check for themselves.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism21/56
I(B) Independence and Objectivity

I(B) recommended procedures

  1. Protect the integrity of opinions: every report reflects the analyst's honest view.
  2. Restricted list for companies the firm will not cover negatively, such as deal clients.
  3. Restrict special cost arrangements: pay for your own travel.
  4. Limit gifts: token items only, with a firm value limit.
  5. Restrict investments: rules on staff buying IPOs and private placements.
  6. Review procedures: supervise compliance with these rules.
  7. Independence policy: a formal written policy on research independence.
  8. Appointed officer: a senior person who oversees independence.
Honest opinions, restricted list, own travel, gift limits, IPO rules, supervision, written policy, an officer in charge.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism22/56
I(B) case pair

Kaju katli or the Maldives?

Case 1. Before Diwali, a broker who wants more of Sharma ji's orders sends a Rs 1,500 box of kaju katli and invites the team to a working dinner. The firm's gift limit is Rs 5,000. Sharma ji accepts both and logs them.

Verdict 1

No violation. Modest, within the firm limit, recorded.

Case 2. The same broker offers Sharma ji and his family a paid weekend at a Maldives resort "to discuss research ideas". He accepts.

Verdict 2

Violation. A lavish gift from someone seeking business could reasonably be expected to compromise where his orders go.

Modest and logged passes; lavish from someone who wants business fails.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism23/56
I(B) case pair

Paid report and the cricket tickets

Case 1. SmallCap Pumps pays Chintu's firm a flat Rs 4 lakh, agreed upfront, for a research report. The fee is the same whatever the rating. The report says Sell and states who paid and how.

Verdict 1

No violation. Flat fee, independent view, full disclosure.

Case 2. Mrs Mehta, a client for ten years, gives Chintu two cricket final tickets after a strong year. He accepts and never tells his firm.

Verdict 2

Violation. Client gifts are allowed, but they must be disclosed to the employer, before accepting where possible.

Payment that cannot bend the view is fine; a client gift hidden from the employer is not.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism24/56
I(B) case pair

The banker and the Buy rating

Case 1. Bankers working on Rasoi Foods' bond issue ask Chintu to keep his Buy. His updated model now says Sell. He changes nothing "to keep the peace".

Verdict 1

Violation. The published rating no longer reflects his honest view.

Case 2. Same pressure. Chintu tells compliance. The firm puts Rasoi on its restricted list and publishes only factual notes until the deal closes.

Verdict 2

No violation. A restricted list avoids publishing biased research.

Never keep a rating you no longer believe; if the firm cannot publish honestly, it should not publish opinions at all.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism25/56
Exam trap

I(B) traps

  • The test is "could reasonably be expected to compromise". Whether you were actually swayed is irrelevant.
  • Client gifts are not banned. Undisclosed ones are the problem.
  • Offering counts as much as accepting. A manager offering a lavish trip to win a mandate violates I(B).
  • Issuer-paid research is allowed; pay contingent on the rating is not.
  • Paying your own way is best practice; company-arranged travel should be modest and is meant for places commercial travel does not reach.
  • Pinky on the yacht: not a member or candidate, so no Standards violation, though firm policy may apply.
Reasonable appearance, disclosure of client gifts, flat fees and modest travel are the I(B) checkpoints.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism26/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

I(C) Misrepresentation, in plain words

Do not knowingly make any misrepresentation about investment analysis, recommendations, actions or other professional activities.

A misrepresentation is any untrue statement, any omission of a fact, or any statement that is otherwise false or misleading. Spoken, written, emailed, in a brochure or on social media: all count.

It covers your qualifications, your firm's services, performance records, and the risk and features of investments.

Anything you knowingly say, write, post or leave out that misleads is a misrepresentation.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism27/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

Omissions, qualifications and outsourced work

  • Omissions: a true statement can still mislead. Model returns shown without the key assumptions, or results from only the best accounts, mislead by leaving facts out.
  • Qualifications: do not overstate degrees, experience, licences or team size.
  • Services: do not claim the firm offers what it cannot deliver.
  • Outsourcing: if research or management is done by outside firms, such as sub-advisers, say so. Presenting it as in-house misrepresents the service.
Half truths, inflated credentials and hidden outsourcing all count as misrepresentation.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism28/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

Guarantees: the most dangerous word in a pitch

You must not guarantee a specific return on investments whose value can fall, like shares or most mutual funds. Promising what markets decide is a misrepresentation.

You may describe a guarantee that really exists in the product, such as a structured note whose issuer promises the principal, or an insured deposit. Describe it accurately, including who stands behind it.

Forecasts are fine when presented as forecasts, not as facts.

Never guarantee a market return; describe a real product guarantee accurately.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism29/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

Plagiarism: copying without credit

Plagiarism means copying or using, in substantially the same form, material others prepared without acknowledging the source and author. It includes:

  • quoting an analyst or report without naming them;
  • paraphrasing someone's analysis as your own;
  • using others' charts, graphs or forecasts without saying where they came from;
  • copying a proprietary spreadsheet or model without permission;
  • putting your name on a third-party report.
Reworded or not, someone else's work without credit is a misrepresentation of whose work it is.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism30/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

Using other people's research the right way

You may use research from outside your firm. Credit it: name the author or source when you quote, paraphrase or summarise. You still judge whether it is sound before relying on it.

The exception: factual information published by recognised financial and statistical reporting services or similar sources, such as prices or reported financials from an established data service, can be used without acknowledgment.

The exception is for facts, not for someone else's analysis, opinions or forecasts.

Credit every borrowed idea; plain facts from recognised reporting services need no footnote.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism31/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

Work done for your employer belongs to the firm

Research and models created while employed belong to the firm.

  • The firm and colleagues can keep using a departed analyst's work, and the firm may issue later reports without crediting the original analyst.
  • You cannot reissue a report someone else wrote under your name alone.
  • You cannot take research or models from an old employer and use them at a new job without permission. That also breaches the duty of loyalty to the old employer.
The firm owns work done on its time; it may reuse it, but no individual may claim it.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism32/56
I(C) Misrepresentation

I(C) recommended procedures

  • Factual presentations: firms give staff a written list of the services the firm offers and its qualifications.
  • Qualification summary: each member keeps an accurate summary of their own qualifications, experience and services.
  • Verify outside information: check that third-party material you pass to clients, such as a product's marketing, is accurate.
  • Maintain webpages: keep websites current and correct.
  • Plagiarism policy: keep copies of sources, attribute direct quotes, attribute paraphrases and summaries.
Write down what you really offer, check what others say about you, and keep your sources.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism33/56
I(C) case pair

Copied chart, cited prices

Case 1. Chintu's cement note lifts three paragraphs and a demand chart from a rival broker's report, with no credit. "The ideas were obvious anyway."

Verdict 1

Violation. Copying others' words and chart without acknowledgment is plagiarism.

Case 2. His next note uses closing prices and quarterly sales from an established market data service without a footnote, and quotes an RBI statement with the source named.

Verdict 2

No violation. Facts from recognised reporting services need no credit; the quote is attributed.

Borrowed analysis needs credit; recognised factual data does not.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism34/56
I(C) case pair

Neha's model and the 12% promise

Case 1. Neha built the firm's auto sector model, then left. Chintu updates it, and the firm keeps publishing the sector report under its own name without naming Neha.

Verdict 1

No violation. Work done for the firm is the firm's property.

Case 2. Sharma ji approves a brochure saying "Our balanced fund guarantees 12% a year." The fund holds shares and bonds.

Verdict 2

Violation. The fund's value can fall. Guaranteeing a return misrepresents it.

Firm property may be reused without credit; market returns may never be guaranteed.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism35/56
Exam trap

I(C) traps

  • "Knowingly": an honest error you did not know about is not a violation, but carrying on once you know makes it knowing.
  • Omissions count. A misleading half truth is still a misrepresentation.
  • Paraphrasing is not a loophole for plagiarism.
  • Facts from recognised data services: no credit. Analysis, opinions, forecasts: credit.
  • A real product guarantee may be described; a market return may not be promised.
  • Misusing the CFA designation falls under VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. Other false credentials fall under I(C).
Knowing, omissions count, paraphrase is still plagiarism, facts are exempt, guarantees only when real.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism36/56
I(D) Misconduct

I(D) Misconduct, in plain words

Do not engage in professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud or deceit, and do not commit any act that reflects adversely on your professional reputation, integrity or competence.

The Standard does not police your private life. Personal behaviour becomes a violation when it involves dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or damages your trustworthiness or ability to do the job.

Conduct can violate I(D) without being illegal.

Dishonesty at work, or anything that undermines trust in you as a professional, is misconduct.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism37/56
I(D) case pair

Long lunches and a peaceful protest

Case 1. Raj, a charterholder and fund manager, drinks heavily at long lunches most days and comes back to place client trades. Errors pile up.

Verdict 1

Violation. The behaviour damages his competence at work and reflects badly on his professional integrity.

Case 2. Sharma ji is arrested at a peaceful protest against cutting trees in a Mumbai forest and released the same day.

Verdict 2

No violation. Peaceful civil disobedience involves no dishonesty and says nothing about his professional integrity or competence.

Ask whether the act touches honesty or fitness for the job, not whether it was embarrassing or even illegal.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism38/56
I(D) case pair

The dinner bill and the failed restaurant

Case 1. Chintu files a family dinner as "client entertainment" on his expense claim.

Verdict 1

Violation. A false expense claim is dishonesty in professional conduct, whatever the amount.

Case 2. Ravi's restaurant side business fails and he files for personal bankruptcy. He hides nothing from creditors.

Verdict 2

No violation. Bankruptcy alone does not reflect on integrity. Hiding assets or lying to creditors would be fraud, and a violation.

Small lies at work are misconduct; honest money trouble is not.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism39/56
Exam trap

I(D) firm procedures and traps

Firms should: adopt a code of ethics; tell staff which acts are violations and what the sanctions are; check references and backgrounds before hiring.

  • Not illegal does not mean no violation: heavy drinking at work can be misconduct.
  • Illegal does not always mean violation: an arrest at a peaceful protest is not.
  • Small amounts do not excuse dishonesty. A Rs 2,000 padded claim is still deceit.
  • Lying on a CV or job application is misconduct.
  • A purely personal dispute or debt problem, with no dishonesty, is usually not misconduct.
Honesty and fitness for the job decide I(D), not legality or the size of the amount.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism40/56
I(E) Competence

I(E) Competence, in plain words

Act with and maintain the competence needed to fulfil your professional responsibilities. This Standard was added in the 2024 update of the Code and Standards.

Competence means the knowledge, skills and abilities your role needs. It has two halves:

  • Act with it: do not take on work you cannot do properly without getting what you need first.
  • Maintain it: keep up as markets, products, rules and tools change.

The bar depends on the role: a bond trader and a wealth adviser need different skills.

Be able to do the job you take on, and stay able as the job changes.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism41/56
I(E) Competence

What staying competent looks like

  • Honestly assess whether you can do a task before taking it on.
  • If not: train first, bring in a qualified colleague or outside expert, or decline.
  • Understand the models, software and data tools you rely on: what they do, their limits, when they fail.
  • Keep learning through continuing education, new rules and new products.

Firms: train staff, give work to people able to do it, and supervise.

Competence differs from diligence: I(E) asks whether you have the ability; V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis asks whether you applied care to a particular analysis.

Assess, close the gap or decline, understand your tools, keep learning.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism42/56
I(E) case pair

The currency options mandate

Case 1. Sharma ji's firm wins a mandate to run a currency options portfolio. Nobody on the team has traded options. Sharma ji accepts and tells Chintu to learn from online videos.

Verdict 1

Violation. He took on responsibilities without the competence to fulfil them and did nothing to close the gap.

Case 2. Same mandate. Before trading, Sharma ji hires an experienced options manager, trains the team, and starts with tight risk limits.

Verdict 2

No violation. He put the needed competence in place before acting.

Taking on work beyond your skills is a violation; closing the gap first is compliance.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism43/56
Exam trap

I(E) traps

  • Competence is not a title. Passing exams does not settle it, and having no charter does not mean incompetence.
  • "Maintain" is ongoing. An adviser still applying tax rules that changed years ago fails it.
  • Getting help is compliance, not weakness: an expert, training first, or declining all satisfy I(E).
  • One honest mistake by a capable person is not automatically a competence failure.
  • Do not mix up I(E) with V(A): ability versus care on one analysis.
Competence is ability kept current, not a credential; getting help counts as meeting it.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism44/56
Which Standard?

Spot which part of Standard I it is

SituationStandard
Keeps sending a deck she knows breaks the rulesI(A)
Takes a lavish trip from a broker seeking ordersI(B)
Calls a share fund "guaranteed"I(C)
Pads an expense claimI(D)
Accepts a mandate nobody can runI(E)

Clue words decide most questions. Check first that the person is a member or candidate.

Law and dissociation: A. Gifts and pressure: B. Untrue or copied: C. Dishonest conduct: D. Skills: E.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism45/56
Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. Standards bind members and candidates only. Pinky can break the law, not the Standards.
  2. I(A): follow the stricter of law and Code; never knowingly help a breach.
  3. Dissociate: compliance first, step away, document, resign last. No duty to tell regulators.
  4. I(B): no offering, soliciting or accepting what could reasonably compromise you. Client gifts: disclose.
  5. Issuer-paid research: flat fee, disclosed. Travel: pay your own way where you can.
  6. I(C): no knowing lies or omissions, no guaranteed market returns, credit others' work. Data-service facts are exempt.
  7. I(D): dishonesty at work or acts that damage professional integrity. Not a peaceful protest arrest.
  8. I(E): be competent for the role and stay so; train, get help or decline.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the chapter summary.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism46/56
Exam question 1 of 10

Kavya, a CFA candidate, works where local law lets analysts accept any gift from issuers. The Code and Standards bar gifts that could reasonably compromise independence. Kavya should follow:

  1. A. local law, because she works there.
  2. B. her employer's policy, whatever it says.
  3. C. the Code and Standards, because they are stricter.
Show answer

Answer: C. I(A) says follow the stricter of the law and the Code; here the Code is stricter. A is wrong because a weaker local law never overrides a stricter Code. B is wrong because an employer policy weaker than the Code does not lower her obligation.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism47/56
Exam question 2 of 10

Arjun, a charterholder, learns that a colleague is backdating trade tickets. His most appropriate first action is to:

  1. A. report it to the securities regulator.
  2. B. raise it with his supervisor or the compliance department.
  3. C. resign from the firm immediately.
Show answer

Answer: B. Dissociation starts with escalating inside the firm. A is not required by the Standards, though a law might require it. C skips the steps: resignation is a last resort if the violation continues.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism48/56
Exam question 3 of 10

Which statement about reporting violations is most accurate under the Code and Standards?

  1. A. Members are not required to report violations to regulators, though it may be appropriate or legally required.
  2. B. Members must report every known legal violation to government authorities.
  3. C. Members must never report outside the firm because of their duty of loyalty.
Show answer

Answer: A. A is right: the Standards require dissociation, not regulatory reporting. B overstates the duty. C is wrong because acting to protect clients or market integrity, not for personal gain, does not breach the duty of loyalty.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism49/56
Exam question 4 of 10

An analyst is hired by a small issuer to write a research report. Which arrangement is most consistent with I(B)?

  1. A. A fee that doubles if the rating is Buy, disclosed in the report.
  2. B. A flat fee with no disclosure, since the analysis is independent anyway.
  3. C. A flat fee agreed in advance, disclosed in the report.
Show answer

Answer: C. C is right: a flat fee, not linked to conclusions, and disclosed. A links pay to the rating, which compromises independence even if disclosed. B fails because the payment must be disclosed so readers can judge the conflict.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism50/56
Exam question 5 of 10

Rohit, a charterholder, receives concert tickets from a long-standing client after a strong year. Rohit should:

  1. A. refuse them, because all gifts are prohibited.
  2. B. accept and disclose them to his employer.
  3. C. accept without telling anyone, because they reward past work.
Show answer

Answer: B. Client gifts for past performance are allowed but must be disclosed to the employer. A is wrong: I(B) does not ban all gifts. C is wrong: past-performance gifts carry less risk, but disclosure is still required.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism51/56
Exam question 6 of 10

Which action is least likely to violate I(C) Misrepresentation?

  1. A. Using share prices from a recognised financial data service without citing it.
  2. B. Including a chart from a broker's report without naming the broker.
  3. C. Rewording another analyst's conclusions and presenting them as your own.
Show answer

Answer: A. Factual information from recognised financial and statistical reporting services may be used without acknowledgment. B and C use others' work without credit, which is plagiarism, and rewording does not cure it.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism52/56
Exam question 7 of 10

Meera built her firm's banking sector model and then left. The firm keeps publishing reports from the model without naming her. The firm's analysts most likely:

  1. A. violated I(C) by not crediting Meera.
  2. B. needed Meera's written consent first.
  3. C. did not violate the Standards, as the work belongs to the firm.
Show answer

Answer: C. Work created for an employer is the firm's property, and later reports need not credit the original analyst. A is wrong for that reason. B is wrong: the departed employee has no ownership to consent with. Reissuing her report under one person's name would be different.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism53/56
Exam question 8 of 10

Which is most likely a violation of I(D) Misconduct?

  1. A. Being arrested at a peaceful environmental protest.
  2. B. Submitting a falsified hotel bill for reimbursement.
  3. C. Filing for personal bankruptcy after a failed business, with full disclosure to creditors.
Show answer

Answer: B. A false expense claim is dishonesty in professional conduct. A is personal civil disobedience with no dishonesty, so not misconduct. C involves no fraud or deceit, so bankruptcy alone does not reflect on integrity.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism54/56
Exam question 9 of 10

A charterholder is offered a mandate in a complex derivatives strategy her team has never used. Which action is most consistent with I(E) Competence?

  1. A. Bring in an experienced specialist and train the team before accepting.
  2. B. Accept, since the CFA charter covers derivatives.
  3. C. Accept and learn on the job using client money.
Show answer

Answer: A. A puts the needed competence in place first. B is wrong: a credential does not prove competence for a specific role. C takes on responsibilities without the competence to fulfil them.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism55/56
Exam question 10 of 10

Pinky, a trader who is neither a CFA Institute member nor a candidate, accepts a lavish yacht trip from a broker seeking her orders. Under the Code and Standards, Pinky:

  1. A. violated I(B) Independence and Objectivity.
  2. B. violated I(D) Misconduct.
  3. C. did not violate the Standards, because they do not apply to her.
Show answer

Answer: C. The Standards bind only members and candidates. A and B would apply to a member or candidate, but not to Pinky. Her firm's gift policy or the law may still apply.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 3: Standard I: Professionalism56/56
Chapter 3 done

Standard I: Professionalism, done

You can now apply all five parts of Standard I: follow the stricter rule and dissociate, keep gifts and pressure from bending judgment, never mislead or plagiarise, stay honest at work, and stay competent. Sharma ji's verdict: "Data dikhao? You just did."

Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets1/43
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • Candidate: anyone enrolled in the CFA Program; bound by the Standards from enrolment.
  • Compliance: the team inside a firm that checks staff follow laws and firm rules.
  • Issuer: the company whose shares or bonds trade in the market.
  • Derivative: a contract whose value comes from another asset, like an option on a share.
  • Liquidity: how easily something trades without moving its price.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets2/43
Story

A tip at the sangeet

A sangeet in Juhu. Between dances, the bride's uncle, CFO of Rasoi Foods, whispers to Pinky: "A takeover offer lands Monday. Shh." Pinky reaches for her trading app. Chintu, a Level I candidate, nearly drops his plate.

Sharma ji, next morning: "Two Standards guard the market itself. II(A) Material Nonpublic Information: do not trade on secrets. II(B) Market Manipulation: do not fake prices or volume."

Pinky is neither a member nor a candidate, so the Standards do not bind her. Insider trading law still does.

Standard II protects the fairness of the market: no trading on secrets, no faking prices or volume.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets3/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, in plain words

A member or candidate who has material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act on it or cause others to act on it.

  • Acting includes buying, selling, and trading related securities or derivatives.
  • Causing others to act includes tipping friends and recommending trades.
  • How you got it does not matter: at work, at a wedding, legally or not.

Both tests must be met: material and nonpublic. Fail either and II(A) does not stop you.

Material plus nonpublic means hands off: no trading, no tipping, no recommending.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets4/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Test 1: is it material?

Information is material if its disclosure would probably affect the price of a security, or if reasonable investors would want to know it before deciding to invest.

  • The more specific the information (amount, date, price), the more likely it is material.
  • The more reliable the source, the more likely it is material. A CFO beats an anonymous chat post.
  • Information already reflected in the price has less value to act on.
Would it move the price, or would a reasonable investor want it? Specific and reliable means material.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets5/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

What usually counts as material

AreaExamples
Company resultsearnings; changes in assets or asset quality
Dealsmergers, acquisitions, tender offers, joint ventures
Businessnew products, patents, regulatory approval or rejection, key customers or suppliers, management or auditor changes
Securitiesdefaults, splits, dividend changes, buybacks, new issues, credit rating changes, bankruptcy, big legal disputes
Marketunreleased government economic data; large trade orders not yet executed
Earnings, deals, approvals, management, securities events, legal fights and pending big orders are the usual suspects.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets6/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Test 2: is it nonpublic?

Information is nonpublic until it has been disseminated to the marketplace in general, so ordinary investors have a fair chance to act on it.

  • Telling a select group, such as a room full of analysts or a few big clients, does not make it public.
  • Public channels: press releases, exchange or regulatory filings, a results call or webcast open to everyone.
  • When unsure whether it is out, assume it is not and check.
Public means released to the whole market, not shared with a lucky few.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets7/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

II(A) decision flowchart

  1. Material? Would it probably move the price, or would a reasonable investor want it? If no, II(A) does not apply. This is where the mosaic theory lives.
  2. Nonpublic? Has it been released to the market in general? If yes, act freely.
  3. If material and nonpublic: do not trade, tip or recommend. Encourage the company to make it public, and tell your compliance department.
Two yeses mean freeze; any no means II(A) is not the obstacle.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets8/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

The mosaic theory

An analyst may combine public information with nonmaterial nonpublic information and act on the conclusion, even if that conclusion would have been material inside information had the company said it directly.

That is the mosaic theory: many small tiles, none of them a secret that moves the price alone, make a picture. The insight comes from the analyst's skill, which is exactly the job.

Keep records of the research behind the conclusion, so you can show how you reached it.

Public pieces plus nonmaterial private pieces make a legal mosaic; one material secret does not.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets9/43
Worked example

Mosaic at work: the cement call

Chintu covers a cement maker. Can he publish a Sell without breaching II(A)?

  1. Public: weak monsoon rainfall data and a cut in the state road budget.
  2. Nonmaterial nonpublic: chats with 12 dealers, each saying stock is moving slowly. None alone moves the price.
  3. Bought data: satellite counts of trucks leaving the plant, sold to any paying client.
  4. Combined: he estimates sales 15% below consensus. He files his notes and models.
Sell is fine: no violation. Had the CFO told him "Q3 is 15% short", that alone would be MNPI.
The mosaic is legal because no single piece was a material secret.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets10/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Selective disclosure and analyst calls

Companies sometimes share news with a few analysts or big investors first. That is selective disclosure, and the information stays nonpublic until the market in general has it.

  • A briefing to a room full of analysts does not make news public.
  • Analysts should notice when they are the chosen few, and not act until it is released.
  • Asking management sharp questions is fine. Acting on a material answer the market has not heard is not.
If you heard it before the market did, it is not public yet.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets11/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Expert networks and company insiders

Expert networks connect analysts with people who know an industry: doctors, engineers, former managers. Using them is allowed.

  • You must not seek or use MNPI from them. An expert running a drug trial who reveals unpublished results has given you MNPI.
  • If you receive it anyway, you cannot act on it.

Insiders include employees, directors, bankers, lawyers and consultants working for the company. Their friends and family pass on the same problem. The source being a relative changes nothing.

Experts for insight, never for secrets; MNPI from anyone is still MNPI.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets12/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Investment research reports

A report or rating change from a well-known analyst can move a price, so in theory it is material. It does not have to be released to the whole market at once.

  • The analyst built it from public and nonmaterial information using skill that clients pay for. Clients may get it first; others can do the work or become clients.
  • Trading ahead of your own firm's unreleased rating change, or ahead of a large client order, is a different problem: it abuses information clients have not yet had.
Distributing research to paying clients first is fine; trading ahead of it is not.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets13/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

You just received MNPI. Now what?

  1. Freeze: do not trade, tip or recommend, for yourself, clients or the firm.
  2. Encourage public disclosure: where appropriate, urge the company to release the information properly.
  3. Tell compliance and no one else.
  4. Compliance decides the next step, such as adding the company to the watch or restricted list.

Once the information is public, normal trading can resume.

Stop, push for disclosure, tell compliance, and say nothing to anyone else.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets14/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Firewalls: keeping secrets where they belong

A firewall (information barrier) keeps MNPI inside the department that legitimately has it, usually investment banking. Key elements:

  • Communication between departments controlled by compliance or legal.
  • Physical separation of departments, and no staff working on both sides.
  • Review of employee trading using watch, restricted and rumour lists.
  • Written procedures, with records of how they are enforced.
  • Closer review or limits on the firm's own trading while it holds MNPI.
Separate the people, control the messages, watch the trades, write it all down.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets15/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

Watch list, restricted list and personal trading

ToolWhat it does
Watch listConfidential list of companies the firm has MNPI about; compliance monitors trading in them
Restricted listShared list; staff and the firm cannot trade, and research may be limited
Personal trading limitsRestrict or ban staff trading in listed names; require reports of staff and family trades

Why keep both? Putting a stock on the restricted list can itself signal that a deal is coming, so the quiet watch list is used first.

Watch list: quiet monitoring. Restricted list: no trading. Staff trades: reported and limited.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets16/43
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information

II(A) recommended procedures

  • Achieve public dissemination: urge the company to release MNPI properly.
  • Compliance procedures to stop misuse, and firewalls that separate departments holding MNPI.
  • Issuers: disclosure procedures and press releases that reach everyone at once.
  • Reporting system: a named compliance person to whom staff report MNPI.
  • Personal and proprietary trading rules, written records, and training for all staff.

A blanket ban on all firm trading while holding MNPI is not always required; a market maker may keep a passive role.

Release it, wall it off, report it, limit trading, record everything, train everyone.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets17/43
II(A) case pair

The wedding tip, two endings

Case 1. At the sangeet, Chintu overhears the CFO tell Pinky a takeover offer for Rasoi Foods lands Monday. On Saturday he buys call options on Rasoi, not the shares: "Derivatives are different."

Verdict 1

Violation. Specific news from the CFO, not yet released: material and nonpublic. Trading derivatives is still acting on it.

Case 2. Same overheard tip. Chintu trades nothing, tells no one, and on Monday morning tells his compliance officer what he heard.

Verdict 2

No violation. He did not act or cause others to act, and he escalated.

MNPI blocks every way of profiting, derivatives included.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets18/43
II(A) case pair

Private call versus open webcast

Case 1. On a one-to-one call, Tyre Co's CFO tells Sharma ji that a key plant will be shut for three months. Nothing is announced. Sharma ji sells the fund's holding that afternoon.

Verdict 1

Violation. Selective disclosure of material news; still nonpublic.

Case 2. Tyre Co announces the shutdown in an exchange filing and explains it on a webcast open to all. Sharma ji sells an hour later.

Verdict 2

No violation. The news is public. Speed after release is skill, not misconduct.

Same fact, different verdict: what matters is whether the market has it.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets19/43
II(A) case pair

The expert and the tip passed on

Case 1. An expert network doctor tells Chintu his hospital's trial of a listed company's new drug has failed. Results are unpublished. Chintu recommends that clients sell.

Verdict 1

Violation. Recommending is causing others to act on MNPI.

Case 2. Chintu passes the Rasoi takeover tip to Pinky, who buys. Chintu buys nothing. Pinky is not a member or candidate.

Verdict 2

Chintu violated II(A): he caused someone else to act. Pinky did not violate the Standards, which do not bind her, but she may have broken insider trading law.

Tipping or recommending is acting; the tippee's status does not save the tipper.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets20/43
Exam trap

II(A) traps

  • Derivatives, related companies and other securities count. Acting is acting.
  • Disclosure to a group of analysts is not public disclosure.
  • Family or friend as the source changes nothing.
  • Tipping or recommending is causing others to act, even with no trade of your own.
  • The mosaic theory needs every private piece to be nonmaterial.
  • A well-known analyst's report going to clients first is not a violation.
  • First action on receiving MNPI: compliance, not the regulator and not your clients.
Options, analyst-only briefings, family sources and tips are all still MNPI problems.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets21/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

II(B) Market Manipulation, in plain words

Do not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants.

  • Information-based: spreading false rumours or misleading information to move a price.
  • Transaction-based: trades that create a false picture of price or activity, or a dominant position used to control a price.

Intent decides. The same trade can be legitimate or manipulative depending on why it was done.

Faking prices or volume to fool the market is manipulation; intent is the dividing line.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets22/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

Information-based manipulation

This is manipulation through what people hear:

  • spreading false rumours, online or offline, to push a price up or down;
  • publishing misleading information or wildly optimistic projections to attract buyers;
  • promoting a stock you are paid to promote without saying so, so investors think the view is independent.

Honest, well-researched opinions are fine, even loud ones, even when you own the stock and disclose it. The problem is information you know is false or misleading.

Moving a price with lies or hype is manipulation; moving it with honest research is analysis.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets23/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

Pump and dump

The classic combination:

  1. Quietly buy a thinly traded stock.
  2. Pump: spread misleading positive information or over-the-top forecasts. Other investors rush in and the price climbs.
  3. Dump: sell at the artificially high price.
  4. The price collapses once the hype fades, and later buyers carry the loss.

The false information makes it information-based; the trading around it shows the intent.

Buy, hype with misleading claims, sell to the people you fooled: textbook II(B).
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets24/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

Transaction-based: fake volume and fake prices

  • Wash trades: buying and selling the same security with no change in who owns it, to create the look of activity.
  • Matched orders with a friend or between accounts you control, for the same effect.
  • Marking the price: small trades at high prices near a valuation date to lift a portfolio's reported value.
  • Any trades designed to give a false impression of price or activity that departs from what a fair market would show.

Other investors see the volume or price, assume real interest, and trade on a fiction.

Trades with no real change of ownership or purpose, made to be seen, are manipulation.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets25/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

Cornering and squeezing a market

Securing a controlling, dominant position in a security or commodity in order to manipulate its price, or the price of a related derivative, is transaction-based manipulation.

Example: a fund quietly buys most of the warehouse stock of a metal deliverable against a futures contract. Short sellers must buy from the fund at whatever price it names. That is a squeeze; owning nearly all the supply is a corner.

Holding a big position is not itself a crime. Using it to dictate prices is.

Size is fine; using dominance to dictate the price is manipulation.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets26/43
II(B) Market Manipulation

Legitimate trading that is not manipulation

II(B) does not ban trading strategies built on perceived market inefficiencies. Intent decides.

StrategyWhy it is fine
Arbitrage across marketsExploits a real price gap; it narrows it
Splitting a block trade over daysAims to reduce price impact, not to mislead
Market makingGenuine quotes and real trades
Big, honest research callTrue information, real reasoning
Real trades for real reasons are fine, even large ones; trades or words designed to deceive are not.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets27/43
II(B) case pair

Month-end bond trades and the big sell order

Case 1. Ravi, a charterholder, runs a fund holding an illiquid corporate bond. On the last day of each month he buys tiny lots at above-market prices, lifting the price used to value the fund.

Verdict 1

Violation. The trades exist to create an artificial price and mislead investors about the fund's value.

Case 2. Sharma ji must sell 5 lakh shares of a mid-cap. To avoid crashing the price, he splits the order over five days.

Verdict 2

No violation. The aim is to reduce market impact, not to mislead anyone.

Trading to create a price is manipulation; trading carefully to avoid moving one is good execution.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets28/43
II(B) case pair

Volume for a rebate, and the NSE and BSE gap

Case 1. An exchange offers lower fees to firms that reach a volume target in a new futures contract. A trading head has two of the firm's accounts trade with each other until the target is met.

Verdict 1

Violation. Wash trading that artificially inflates volume and misleads others about real interest.

Case 2. Chintu spots a share at Rs 500 on one exchange and Rs 503 on the other. He buys on the first and sells on the second at the same moment.

Verdict 2

No violation. Arbitrage on a real price gap; it helps close the gap.

Volume that changes no ownership is fake; trades that exploit a real gap are legitimate.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets29/43
II(B) case pair

The takeover rumour and the honest post

Case 1. Chintu buys a small-cap, then posts on social media that a takeover is coming. He has no source. The price jumps and he sells.

Verdict 1

Violation. Information-based manipulation: a pump and dump on a false rumour.

Case 2. Chintu posts his researched view that a stock is undervalued, links his model, and says he owns it. The price rises.

Verdict 2

No violation. Honest, disclosed analysis, with no intent to mislead.

Same stock, same rising price: lies make it manipulation, honest research does not.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets30/43
Exam trap

II(B) traps

  • Intent is required. A large trade that moves the price is not manipulation if the aim was not to mislead.
  • Information-based needs no trading by you; spreading the rumour is enough.
  • Wash trades are manipulation even if the price barely moves: fake volume misleads too.
  • Owning a stock and praising it honestly, with disclosure, is not manipulation.
  • Trading on a secret is II(A); faking prices or volume is II(B). Pick the right one.
No intent to mislead, no II(B); false words or fake trades with that intent, II(B).
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets31/43
Which Standard?

II(A), II(B) or neither?

SituationAnswer
Sells after a CFO's private hint of a missII(A)
Posts a made-up takeover rumourII(B)
Two own accounts trade to inflate volumeII(B)
Sells on a mosaic of public and nonmaterial dataNeither
Splits a large order over daysNeither

Check first that the person is a member or candidate.

Secrets: II(A). Fakery: II(B). Skill and honest trades: neither.
Ch 4: Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets32/43
Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. II(A): material and nonpublic means no trading, tipping or recommending, derivatives included.
  2. Material: would probably move the price, or a reasonable investor would want it. Specific and reliable means more material.
  3. Nonpublic until released to the market in general. A briefing to analysts is not public.
  4. Mosaic: public plus nonmaterial nonpublic pieces may be combined and acted on. Keep records.
  5. On getting MNPI: freeze, encourage public disclosure, tell compliance only.
  6. Firewalls, a quiet watch list, a restricted list and staff trading limits keep MNPI contained.
  7. II(B): distorting prices or inflating volume with intent to mislead. Information-based or transaction-based.
  8. Not manipulation: arbitrage, splitting big orders, honest disclosed research.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the chapter summary.

Exam question 1 of 10

Which information is most likely material?

  1. A. A CFO's statement that a takeover offer at a stated price will be signed on Monday.
  2. B. An anonymous chat post saying "something big is coming".
  3. C. A rumour that is already fully reflected in the share price.
Show answer

Answer: A. A is specific and from a reliable source, so it would probably move the price. B is vague and unreliable, so less likely material. C has little value because the market has already priced it.

Exam question 2 of 10

On a private call, a CFO tells 20 analysts that quarterly sales will fall sharply. Nothing has been announced. The information is most likely:

  1. A. public, because 20 analysts heard it.
  2. B. nonpublic, because it has not been released to the market in general.
  3. C. public as soon as any analyst publishes a note.

Answer: B. Selective disclosure to a group does not make information public. A is wrong: a room of analysts is not the market. C is wrong: one analyst's note to clients is not general release.

Exam question 3 of 10

An analyst combines public reports, satellite truck counts sold to any buyer, and chats with dealers that each reveal little, and concludes earnings will miss. She issues a Sell. She most likely:

  1. A. violated II(A), because her conclusion is material.
  2. B. violated II(A), because the dealer chats were nonpublic.
  3. C. did not violate II(A), under the mosaic theory.
Show answer

Answer: C. The mosaic theory allows acting on conclusions built from public and nonmaterial nonpublic information. A is wrong: a material conclusion is fine if no input was MNPI. B is wrong: the dealer chats were nonpublic but nonmaterial.

  2. B. Review of employee trading using watch and restricted lists.

Why do firms often use a confidential watch list rather than only a restricted list?

  1. A. Adding a stock to a restricted list can itself signal that the firm holds MNPI.

A trading head has two of the firm's accounts trade a new futures contract with each other to qualify for an exchange's volume-based fee discount. This most likely:
