Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients1/56
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • Member, candidate: a CFA Institute member, or someone registered for a CFA exam.
  • Brokerage: the commission a broker charges to execute a trade; on a client's trade, the client pays.
  • Proxy: a vote attached to shares, cast at a company's shareholder meeting.
  • IPO: initial public offering: a company's first sale of shares to the public.
  • Mandate: the written rules for what a fund may hold, e.g. 'large-cap Indian equities'.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients2/56
Story

Whose money is it, anyway?

Monday, a Mumbai investment firm. Chintu, a Level I candidate, gets his first client files. Pinky, the trader, has a tip: "Trade Mrs Desai's account a bit more. Diwali bonus target, na?"

Sharma ji, CFA charterholder and CIO, shuts the file. "Her money. Her interests. Before the firm's, and long before yours." Then he writes the five parts of Standard III: Duties to Clients:

  1. III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
  2. III(B) Fair Dealing
  3. III(C) Suitability
  4. III(D) Performance Presentation
  5. III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
Standard III asks one question five ways: did the client's interest come first?
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients3/56
The Standard

III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care

In plain words: you owe clients a duty of loyalty, you must act with reasonable care, and you must use prudent judgment. Act for the client's benefit, and put the client's interests before your employer's and your own.

  • Loyalty: no self-dealing, no hidden agenda.
  • Prudence: caution and discretion, as with someone else's savings.
  • Care: the attention a prudent professional would give in the same role.

III(A) does not make every member a legal fiduciary (someone the law requires to act in another's best interest). Where law or the role does impose fiduciary duties, meet those too.

Order of duties: client first, employer second, you last.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients4/56
Guidance

Who is the client? Know the scope

Loyalty needs a target. Identify the real client and the scope of your role.

SituationThe client is
Company pension planthe plan's participants and beneficiaries, not the company's management
Trustthe beneficiaries
Fund run to a mandatethe fund's investors as a group: manage to the stated mandate
Individual accountthat person

Scope: are you advising with discretion, or only executing orders? Know what you agreed to do, and do that with loyalty, prudence and care.

For a pension plan, loyalty runs to the beneficiaries, not to the company that hired you.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients5/56
Guidance

Developing the client's portfolio

Care in practice means running the portfolio the way the client's situation demands:

  • Learn the client's objectives and constraints before acting, then follow them.
  • Diversify to reduce risk, unless the mandate says otherwise.
  • Judge each holding in the context of the whole portfolio.
  • Review the account regularly.
  • Never trade just to earn commissions (churning). Every trade must serve the client.

Prudence is not zero risk. A risky asset can be prudent inside a diversified portfolio that suits the client.

Care means a process: know, follow, diversify, review, and trade only for the client.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients6/56
Guidance

Client brokerage belongs to the client

Commissions paid on a client's trades are the client's money. Core rule: client brokerage is the property of the client.

  • Soft commissions (soft dollars): the broker bundles research with execution. Allowed only if the research helps you make investment decisions for the clients whose trades paid for it.
  • Not allowed: using client brokerage for things that benefit the firm or you, such as office costs or buying client referrals.
  • Directed brokerage: a client may tell you which broker to use. Follow it, and disclose that this may cost them best execution.
Soft dollars must buy something that helps the clients who paid them.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients7/56
Worked example

Best execution is not the cheapest commission

Best execution means the best total result for the client: price, commission, market impact, speed and certainty together. Chintu must buy Rs 1 crore of shares. Broker A charges 0.05% commission but its clumsy order handling moves the price 0.40%. Broker B charges 0.10% and moves the price 0.15%.

  1. Broker A: commission Rs 5,000 + price impact Rs 40,000 = Rs 45,000.
  2. Broker B: commission Rs 10,000 + price impact Rs 15,000 = Rs 25,000.
  3. B costs the client Rs 20,000 less, despite double the commission.
Best execution: Broker B, total cost Rs 25,000.
Seek the best total outcome for the client, not the lowest commission line.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients8/56
Guidance

Proxy voting is part of loyalty

Shares carry votes, and votes have economic value. When you manage a client's shares, loyalty covers how you vote them.

  • Vote proxies in an informed, responsible way, in the client's interest. Never to please a company that gives your firm business.
  • A cost-benefit view is allowed: voting every routine proxy may not benefit the client. Votes that change value, such as mergers, takeovers or board contests, deserve real analysis.
  • Have written proxy voting policies and disclose them to clients.
Vote proxies for the client's benefit under a disclosed policy; skipping a routine vote can be fine.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients9/56
Recommended procedures

III(A): how to comply

The handbook's list for members and candidates:

  • Follow the rules and policies that govern the client's mandate; know the applicable law.
  • Set the investment objectives with the client, and stick to them.
  • Diversify; deal fairly with all clients; review accounts regularly.
  • Disclose conflicts of interest, and how you and your firm are paid.
  • Vote proxies in the client's interest; seek best execution.
  • Keep client information confidential.
  • When in doubt, put the client's interests first.
III(A) procedures boil down to: know the client, follow the mandate, disclose, and put the client first.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients10/56
Case

Case: the referral broker

Sharma ji routes all his clients' trades to Lotus Securities, whose commissions are 30% above the market. Lotus gives no research and no better execution, but it refers wealthy customers to Sharma ji's firm. Did Sharma ji most likely violate III(A)?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation. Client brokerage belongs to the clients. Sharma ji spent it to win new business for his firm, a benefit to the firm, not to the clients who paid. He also ignored best execution.

Paying with client commissions for the firm's marketing breaks the duty of loyalty.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients11/56
Case

Case: the client picks the broker

Mrs Kapoor tells Chintu to send all her trades to her nephew's brokerage. Its execution is slower than the firm's usual brokers. Chintu explains, in writing, that she may not get best execution and may pay more. She confirms her instruction in writing, and Chintu follows it. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. Her brokerage is her property, so she may direct it. Chintu disclosed the possible cost of the arrangement and followed the client's informed instruction. That is directed brokerage done right.

A client may direct her own brokerage; your job is to disclose what it may cost her.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients12/56
Exam trap

III(A) traps

  • For a pension plan, the client is the beneficiaries, not the sponsor's management or whoever hired you.
  • Best execution is the best total outcome, not the lowest commission.
  • Soft dollars may buy research that helps the paying clients; never rent, salaries or referrals.
  • Not voting a routine proxy can be fine (cost-benefit). Voting to please a company for business is not.
  • An employer's instruction never overrides the client's interests.
  • Prudence is not avoiding all risk.
When a choice helps the firm or you at the client's cost, III(A) is in play.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients13/56
The Standard

III(B) Fair Dealing

In plain words: deal fairly and objectively with all clients when you provide investment analysis, make investment recommendations, take investment action, or do other professional work.

Fair, not necessarily equal. You cannot reach every client in the same second, and clients with different mandates hold different things. The test: no client is favoured or hurt, on purpose or through a sloppy process.

It covers two things: investment recommendations (the advice) and investment actions (the trades).

Fair dealing means no client gets an unfair head start, not that everyone gets the identical thing.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients14/56
Guidance

Recommendations, actions, and changes

  • Recommendations: get each one to all clients who have shown interest or for whom it may be suitable, so all have a fair chance to act. Same instant by same channel is not required; a process that favours no group is.
  • Changes to a recommendation matter as much as the original. Tell clients, especially those who acted on the earlier advice.
  • If a client who has not heard the change wants to trade on the old view, tell them about the change before you accept the order.
  • Actions: allocate block trades and new issues fairly, at the same price.
A changed rating needs the same fair dissemination as the first one.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients15/56
Guidance

IPOs and hot issues

A hot issue is a new issue so popular that the firm gets fewer shares than clients want.

  • Allocate it fairly among clients who asked and for whom it is suitable, usually pro rata to their orders.
  • Do not take it for yourself, your family or the firm while client orders go unfilled.
  • Do not use it to reward big clients or lure new ones.
  • Family members who are fee-paying clients are treated like any other client: no extra, no less.
Clients first on hot issues; members' own accounts wait until client orders are filled.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients16/56
Worked example

Pro rata allocation of a hot issue

Clients A, B and C order 12,000, 6,000 and 2,000 shares of a hot IPO. Chintu's firm receives only 8,000 shares. Allocate pro rata.

  1. Total ordered = 12,000 + 6,000 + 2,000 = 20,000.
  2. Fill ratio = 8,000 / 20,000 = 40%.
  3. A: 12,000 x 40% = 4,800. B: 6,000 x 40% = 2,400. C: 2,000 x 40% = 800.
  4. Check: 4,800 + 2,400 + 800 = 8,000. Every client gets the same price.
A 4,800, B 2,400, C 800: each gets 40% of the order.
Pro rata means the same fill percentage for every client, at the same price.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients17/56
Guidance

Premium service levels

Firms may sell different levels of service: a premium tier with weekly calls, deeper reports or a dedicated manager. That is fair if:

  • the levels and their fees are disclosed to clients and prospects;
  • the premium level is available to every client willing to pay for it;
  • it does not disadvantage other clients. For example, premium clients must not get a rating change early enough to trade ahead of everyone else.

Charging more for more service is fair. Quietly serving some clients first is not.

Tiered service is fine when disclosed, open to all, and harmless to the other tiers.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients18/56
Recommended procedures

III(B): how to comply

  • Limit how many people know about a recommendation before release.
  • Shorten the time between the decision and its release.
  • Publish guidelines for staff before release: no trading on it, no tipping.
  • Release to all clients at the same time where possible.
  • Keep a list of clients and holdings, so changes reach those affected.
  • Write trade allocation procedures: advance indications of interest for new issues, pro rata at the same execution price, round lots, and time-stamped orders executed in the order received.
  • Review accounts systematically; disclose allocation rules and service levels.
Few insiders, short gap, written allocation rules, time-stamped orders.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients19/56
Case

Case: big clients first

The research team downgrades Ravi Motors from buy to sell at 10:00. Sharma ji phones his five largest clients at 10:05. The email to all other clients goes out at 15:00, by which time the stock has fallen 6%. Did Sharma ji most likely violate the Standards?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation of III(B) Fair Dealing. Size does not buy a head start on a change in recommendation. A material change must reach all interested clients through a process that gives each a fair chance to act. The five-hour gap hurt every client who heard late.

A rating change is dealt fairly or not at all; big clients get no head start.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients20/56
Case

Case pair: the hot IPO and the family

A hot IPO arrives; the firm gets one third of what clients ordered.

Case 1. Sharma ji fills his wife's personal brokerage account (she is not a client) in full, then splits the rest among clients.

Verdict, case 1

Violation. A member's family account jumped ahead of unfilled client orders. Clients come first on hot issues.

Case 2. Chintu's mother is a fee-paying client with the same mandate as others. She gets the same pro rata fill as everyone.

Verdict, case 2

No violation. A family member who is a genuine client is treated like any other client: no extra, and no less.

Family accounts that are real clients are treated like every other client.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients21/56
Exam trap

III(B) traps

  • "Fair" does not mean "equal" or "in the same second". It means no one is systematically favoured.
  • Large or long-standing clients get no head start on recommendations, changes or IPOs.
  • Premium service is fine only if disclosed, open to all who pay, and harmless to others.
  • Members' own and family accounts wait behind clients on hot issues; family members who are real clients are treated equally.
  • A client about to trade on stale advice must hear about the change first.
Look for a client who got there first for no fair reason: that is the III(B) violation.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients22/56
The Standard

III(C) Suitability

Part 1. In an advisory relationship, you must:

  • make reasonable inquiry into the client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints before advising or acting, and reassess this regularly;
  • check that each investment suits the client's financial situation and fits their written objectives, mandates and constraints;
  • judge suitability in the context of the client's total portfolio.

Part 2. When managing a portfolio to a stated mandate, strategy or style, only recommend or act in line with that portfolio's stated objectives and constraints.

Suitability: fit the person in advisory work, fit the mandate in a fund.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients23/56
Guidance

Knowing the client: objectives and constraints

Before advising, find out:

ItemAsk
Returnwhat return the client needs and wants
Riskability to bear risk (wealth, income, horizon) and willingness (attitude)
Liquidity, time horizoncash needs soon; how long the money is invested
Taxes, legaltax position; laws and rules on the account
Uniqueanything else, e.g. no tobacco shares, a family business stake

Plus the client's investment experience. A first-time investor needs more explanation than a fund veteran.

Two objectives (return, risk) and five constraints (liquidity, horizon, taxes, legal, unique).
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients24/56
Guidance

The investment policy statement, kept current

The investment policy statement (IPS) is the written plan agreed with the client. It usually covers:

  • client identification: type and nature of the client;
  • objectives: return and risk;
  • constraints: liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal, unique needs;
  • the benchmark used to measure performance.

Update it at least annually, and whenever the client's circumstances change materially: marriage, a child, job loss, an inheritance, retirement. Review it before making material changes to the advice.

Review the IPS at least once a year and at every material change in the client's life.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients25/56
Guidance

Unsolicited trades: still your problem

A client calls with her own idea: "Put Rs 20 lakh into SmallCap Space Ltd." This is an unsolicited trade, and suitability still applies.

  • Unsuitable but a small effect on the whole portfolio: you may execute after explaining the concern, and document that the client asked for it.
  • Unsuitable and it would materially change the portfolio: discuss it. If the client's goals have truly changed, update the IPS; otherwise the firm may decline the order.
Clients may break their own plan, but only after you have explained and documented it.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients26/56
Guidance

Managing a fund to its stated mandate

When you run a fund or account to a stated mandate, the mandate is the client's instruction.

  • A large-cap Indian equity fund holds large-cap Indian equities. Adding small caps or crypto because they look exciting breaks the mandate, even if they make money.
  • You are not judging whether the fund suits each investor. That is the investor's call, or their adviser's.
  • If the strategy must change, tell investors in advance so they can decide whether to stay.
In a mandated fund, suitability means sticking to the mandate, win or lose.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients27/56
Recommended procedures

III(C): how to comply

  • Write an IPS for every advisory client: client identification, objectives, constraints, and the performance benchmark.
  • Update it regularly: at least annually, and before material changes to the advice. Also when the client's situation changes.
  • Suitability test policies: check every recommendation against the IPS and the effect on the total portfolio, including risk and concentration.
  • Record unsolicited trade requests and the discussion about them.
  • For mandated funds: write the mandate down, monitor drift, and notify investors before any change.
No IPS, no suitability: write it, test against it, update it.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients28/56
Case

Case: the retiree and the futures

Mrs Fernandes, 68, retired, lives on her portfolio's income. Her IPS says low risk, income focus. Pinky pitches a leveraged futures strategy. Chintu, keen to impress, moves 40% of her money into it without discussing it with her. Who most likely violated III(C)?

Verdict (tap to see)

Chintu violated III(C). As a candidate he is bound by the Standards. The trade ignores her objectives and constraints and contradicts her IPS. Pinky did not violate the Standards: she is not a member or candidate, so they do not bind her, though firm rules may.

Suitability is tested against the client's IPS; candidates are bound, non-members are not.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients29/56
Case

Case: a risky stock in a sturdy portfolio

Arjun, 29, software engineer, high income, 30-year horizon. His IPS: aggressive growth, diversified, high risk tolerance. Chintu buys a 2% position in a newly listed, very volatile biotech start-up. On its own the stock is far riskier than the market. Violation of III(C)?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. Suitability is judged in the context of the total portfolio. A small position that fits an aggressive, diversified IPS is suitable even if the stock alone is very risky.

Judge a holding by what it does to the whole portfolio, not by its risk alone.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients30/56
Exam trap

III(C) traps

  • "Risky investment = unsuitable" is wrong. Judge it in the total portfolio.
  • Making money does not cure a mandate breach.
  • A fund manager is not checking suitability for each investor, only sticking to the mandate.
  • Update the IPS at least annually and on material change, not "every three years" or "only when asked".
  • Unsolicited trades still need a suitability conversation and a record.
  • Inquiry comes before advice or action, not after.
III(C) answers hinge on three words: before, total portfolio, mandate.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients31/56
The Standard

III(D) Performance Presentation

In plain words: when you communicate investment performance, make reasonable efforts to ensure it is fair, accurate and complete.

It covers any performance you share: pitch decks, factsheets, a WhatsApp to a prospect, a line in a speech. Your own record, your firm's, or a fund's.

The Standard does not require compliance with GIPS (the Global Investment Performance Standards), but GIPS is the recommended way to meet it.

True numbers chosen to impress can still be unfair.

Every performance number you share must be fair, accurate and complete, GIPS or not.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients32/56
Worked example

Cherry-picking and the missing account

Five accounts follow one strategy. Start values (Rs crore) and returns: A 10 at +24%, B 20 at +15%, C 30 at +11%, D 20 at +6%, E 20 at -12%. Client E left after the loss. Which number may the brochure show?

  1. Best account alone: 24%. Cherry-picked.
  2. Survivors A to D, weighted by value: (240 + 300 + 330 + 120) / 80 = 12.4%. Drops the loser.
  3. All five: (240 + 300 + 330 + 120 - 240) / 100 = 7.5%. Includes the terminated account for the period it was managed.
Fair figure: 7.5%, from all accounts, including the one that left.
Terminated accounts stay in the history; one star account is not the record.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients33/56
Guidance

Simulated results, disclosures, short formats

  • Simulated, model or backtested results may be shown only if clearly labelled as hypothetical, with the method explained. Passing a backtest off as real is a violation.
  • Disclose what a reader needs: gross or net of fees, leverage or derivatives used, the benchmark, the period, and whether terminated accounts are excluded.
  • Brief presentations (an ad, a tweet) are fine if they say they are limited and offer full details on request.
  • Show a composite of all similar portfolios, not one "representative" account.
Label simulations, disclose the assumptions, and offer the full story on request.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients34/56
Recommended procedures

III(D): how to comply

  • Apply GIPS. The most direct route to fair, accurate and complete.
  • Consider the knowledge and sophistication of the audience.
  • Present the weighted composite of similar portfolios, not a single account.
  • Include terminated accounts in historical results, and say clearly when any are excluded.
  • Include disclosures that explain the numbers: gross or net of fees, assumptions, other relevant factors.
  • Keep the data and records used to calculate the performance.
GIPS, composites, terminated accounts, disclosures, records.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients35/56
Case

Case: the track record that moved firms

Sharma ji joins Lotus AMC, which was founded eight months ago. Its brochure says: "Lotus Growth Strategy: 19% a year for 5 years." The 19% was earned by Sharma ji's team at his previous firm. The brochure does not say so. Did Sharma ji most likely violate III(D)?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation. Presenting another firm's history as Lotus's own is not fair, accurate or complete. A track record earned elsewhere could be shown only if clearly described as such, with the records to support it.

A track record belongs to where it was earned; say so or do not show it.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients36/56
Case

Case: the labelled backtest

Chintu builds a quant "monsoon momentum" model in 2026 and backtests it from 2010. His slide says: "Hypothetical backtested results, not actual trading. Gross of fees. Model built in 2026 using past data." His short post on social media reads: "Backtest: 14% a year. Hypothetical; full method on our site." Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. The simulated results are clearly labelled, with key limits disclosed. The short post flags its limited nature and points to the full information.

Simulated numbers are allowed when they are labelled as simulated, with details available.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients37/56
Exam trap

III(D) traps

  • III(D) does not require GIPS compliance. It requires fair, accurate, complete.
  • Dropping terminated or losing accounts (survivorship bias) is a violation.
  • Choosing the flattering period or the best account is a violation, even if every number is true.
  • Backtests are fine when clearly labelled as simulated.
  • A short ad is fine when it says full details are available on request.
  • It applies to anyone who communicates performance, not only the marketing team.
If a true number was chosen to mislead, III(D) is violated.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients38/56
The Standard

III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality

In plain words: keep information about current, former and prospective clients confidential, unless:

  1. the information concerns illegal activities by the client;
  2. disclosure is required by law; or
  3. the client or prospective client permits the disclosure.

The duty does not end when the client leaves. A prospect who never signed up is protected too.

Three exceptions only: illegal activity, required by law, client permission.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients39/56
Guidance

Law, the PCP, and data

  • Laws may require you to report, for example suspected money laundering. Follow them, and ask compliance or legal counsel.
  • CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program (PCP), which investigates possible breaches: giving confidential client information to the PCP in an investigation is not a violation. The PCP keeps it confidential.
  • Electronic data: follow your firm's rules for storing and sending client information. Take reasonable care against leaks: no client files on personal email.
  • The duty covers what you learn through the client relationship.
Cooperating with the PCP or obeying the law is never a III(E) breach.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients40/56
Recommended procedures

III(E): how to comply

  • The simplest, safest route: do not disclose client information, except to colleagues who also work for that client.
  • If you want to share something outside the relationship and no law is involved, discuss it with the client first.
  • Communicate with clients through secure, approved methods, and follow the firm's procedures for electronic data.
  • When unsure whether an exception applies, ask compliance or legal before speaking.
Default to silence; disclose only under an exception or with the client's say-so.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients41/56
Case

Case: wedding gossip

At a cousin's wedding in Jaipur, guests ask Sharma ji about a film star who was his client until two years ago. Sharma ji: "Lost crores on his Goa villa bets, poor man. He had to sell two." Nothing illegal is involved, and the star never agreed to this. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation of III(E). Former clients are protected. None of the three exceptions applies: no illegal activity, no legal requirement, no permission. Fame and juicy stories are not exceptions.

Former clients keep their confidentiality forever; fame is not an exception.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients42/56
Case

Case: the regulator and the PCP

The securities regulator issues a formal order requiring Chintu's firm to produce a client's trading records for an insider trading probe. The firm complies. Separately, the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program asks Chintu about a complaint, and he shares the relevant client details. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation in either. The first disclosure is required by law, one of the three exceptions. The second is cooperation with the PCP, which the Standard expressly allows.

Disclosing because the law requires it, or to the PCP, is allowed.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients43/56
Case

Case: Pinky's WhatsApp

Pinky posts a screenshot of a well-known client's holdings in her college WhatsApp group: "Guess whose portfolio?" Pinky is not a CFA Institute member or candidate. Sharma ji, her supervisor and a charterholder, finds out. Did Pinky violate the Code and Standards?

Verdict (tap to see)

No, not the Code and Standards: they bind only members and candidates, and Pinky is neither. She has likely broken firm policy and perhaps the law, and the firm can discipline her. Sharma ji, who supervises her, must now act under IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors.

The Standards bind members and candidates; their supervisors answer for the rest.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients44/56
Exam trap

III(E) traps

  • Former and prospective clients are protected, not only current ones.
  • Exactly three exceptions: illegal activity, required by law, client permission. Nothing else.
  • Sharing with the CFA Institute PCP is allowed.
  • Disclosing illegal activity is permitted by the Standard; local law may make it mandatory.
  • Only members and candidates can violate the Standards; a non-member's leak is a supervision issue for the member.
Run every disclosure through the three exceptions; if none fits, it is a violation.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients45/56
Sharma ji's red pen

7 things to remember

  1. Clients, then employer, then you. Pension plan client = beneficiaries.
  2. Client brokerage is the client's. Best execution = total cost.
  3. Proxies: vote for the client under a disclosed policy.
  4. Fair, not equal. Hot issues pro rata; members' accounts last.
  5. Suitability: ask first, judge the total portfolio, obey the mandate. IPS yearly and on change.
  6. Performance: fair, accurate, complete; keep terminated accounts; label simulations.
  7. Confidentiality: illegal activity, required by law, or client permission. PCP is fine.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the back of a client file.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients46/56
Exam question 1 of 10

A manager runs a company's defined benefit pension plan. Under III(A), her duty of loyalty is owed primarily to:

  1. A. the company's management, who appointed her.
  2. B. the plan's participants and beneficiaries.
  3. C. her own firm, which employs her.
Show answer

Answer: B. For a pension plan, the ultimate clients are the participants and beneficiaries whose retirement money it is. A is wrong: management hires the manager but is not the client. C is wrong: the employer ranks behind clients in the order of duties.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients47/56
Exam question 2 of 10

Which use of client brokerage is most likely consistent with the Standards?

  1. A. Paying higher commissions to a broker who refers new clients to the firm.
  2. B. Using commissions to pay part of the firm's office rent.
  3. C. Using commissions to buy research that helps manage the accounts that paid them.
Show answer

Answer: C. Client brokerage belongs to the client, so it may buy research that assists investment decisions for those clients. A spends client money on the firm's marketing. B spends it on the firm's overheads. Both benefit the firm, not the clients.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients48/56
Exam question 3 of 10

Chintu must buy Rs 2 crore of shares. Broker X charges 0.08% commission with expected price impact of 0.30%. Broker Y charges 0.15% with expected price impact of 0.12%. Which choice best reflects best execution?

  1. A. Broker X, because its commission is lower.
  2. B. Broker Y, total expected cost Rs 54,000.
  3. C. Broker X, total expected cost Rs 76,000.
Show answer

Answer: B. Total cost: X = 0.38% of Rs 2 crore = Rs 76,000; Y = 0.27% = Rs 54,000. Y is cheaper overall. A looks only at commission, which is not best execution. C states X's cost correctly but it is the more expensive choice.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients49/56
Exam question 4 of 10

An analyst changes her rating on a stock from buy to sell. Which action is most consistent with III(B) Fair Dealing?

  1. A. Release the change to all clients at the same time electronically, then call clients who hold the stock.
  2. B. Call the firm's ten largest clients first, then email everyone else later that day.
  3. C. Wait until the firm's own account has sold before telling clients.
Show answer

Answer: A. A gives every client a fair chance to act, then adds follow-up for the holders most affected. B gives big clients a head start, which disadvantages the rest. C puts the firm ahead of clients, which also breaks the order of duties.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients50/56
Exam question 5 of 10

A firm receives 6,000 shares of an oversubscribed IPO. Client orders: A 10,000, B 4,000, C 1,000. Under a pro rata policy, Client B most likely receives:

  1. A. 1,600 shares.
  2. B. 2,000 shares.
  3. C. 4,000 shares.
Show answer

Answer: A. Fill ratio = 6,000 / 15,000 = 40%, so B gets 4,000 x 40% = 1,600. B splits the issue equally three ways, which ignores order size. C fills B in full, which would leave too little for the others and favours B.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients51/56
Exam question 6 of 10

Under III(C), an advisory client's investment policy statement should most likely be reviewed:

  1. A. every three years, as a standard cycle.
  2. B. only when the client asks for a review.
  3. C. at least annually and when the client's circumstances change materially.
Show answer

Answer: C. The guidance calls for regular updates, at least annually, and whenever material changes occur. A is too infrequent. B puts the burden on the client; the manager must reassess regularly.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients52/56
Exam question 7 of 10

A portfolio manager runs a fund with a stated mandate of investment-grade bonds. She learns that one investor is 25 and wants aggressive growth. She should most likely:

  1. A. keep managing the fund to its stated mandate.
  2. B. add high-yield bonds and equities to suit that investor.
  3. C. ask the investor to sell, because the fund is unsuitable for him.
Show answer

Answer: A. When managing to a mandate, the duty is to stay consistent with the fund's stated objectives; suitability for each investor is the investor's or his adviser's decision. B breaks the mandate for every other investor. C is not required by the Standards.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients53/56
Exam question 8 of 10

Three equal-sized accounts follow one strategy. Returns: +18%, +10%, and -8% for an account the client closed at year end. A brochure shows 14%. A fair, complete composite return is closest to:

  1. A. 18.0%
  2. B. 14.0%
  3. C. 6.7%
Show answer

Answer: C. Including all accounts: (18 + 10 - 8) / 3 = 6.7%. A is the best single account, cherry-picked. B averages only the two surviving accounts and drops the terminated loser, which is survivorship bias.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients54/56
Exam question 9 of 10

Which of the following is least likely to violate III(D) Performance Presentation?

  1. A. Presenting the best-performing account as "representative" of the strategy.
  2. B. Showing backtested results clearly labelled as hypothetical, with the method disclosed.
  3. C. Leaving closed accounts out of the historical record without saying so.
Show answer

Answer: B. Clearly labelled simulated results with disclosed methods are allowed. A cherry-picks one account instead of a composite. C hides terminated accounts, making the record unfair and incomplete.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients55/56
Exam question 10 of 10

Which disclosure of client information most likely violates III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality?

  1. A. Giving client details to the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program during an investigation.
  2. B. Producing a client's records in response to a court order.
  3. C. Telling friends at dinner about the portfolio of a client who left the firm last year.
Show answer

Answer: C. Former clients are protected and none of the exceptions applies to dinner gossip. A is expressly allowed: cooperating with the PCP is not a violation. B is disclosure required by law, one of the three exceptions.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 5: Standard III: Duties to Clients56/56
Chapter 5 done

Clients first, five ways

Chintu can now spot a III(A) brokerage abuse, an unfair rating release, an unsuitable trade, a cherry-picked track record and a leaky mouth at a wedding. Sharma ji handed him Mrs Desai's file and said, "Her interests. First." Chintu said it back. Sharma ji almost smiled.

Swipe on, or jump to another chapter from the Menu.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis1/55
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • Member, candidate: a CFA Institute member, or someone registered for a CFA exam.
  • Compliance: the team that writes and polices a firm's rules for staff.
  • Non-compete: a contract that stops an ex-employee competing for a set time.
  • Third-party research: analysis bought or borrowed from outside, e.g. a broker's report.
  • Front-running: trading for yourself just ahead of a client's large order.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis2/55
Story

The job offer and the client list

Friday evening. Chintu, a Level I candidate, gets an offer from a rival fund: 40% more pay. Pinky, the trader, leans over: "Download the client list tonight. And copy your Excel models. Old firm will never know."

Sharma ji, CFA charterholder and CIO, overhears. "Two Standards in one sentence, Pinky. IV: Duties to Employers, and V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions. Chintu, sit. Data dikhao, and I mean the rules."

This chapter covers IV(A), IV(B), IV(C), V(A), V(B) and V(C).

Standards IV and V: be loyal to the firm that pays you, and do honest, documented analysis.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis3/55
The Standard

IV(A) Loyalty

In plain words: in matters related to your employment, act for the benefit of your employer. Do not deprive it of your skills and abilities, do not divulge its confidential information, and do not otherwise cause it harm.

Limits of the duty:

  • It is not blind obedience. If the employer's interest conflicts with the Code and Standards or with clients' interests, those win.
  • You need not give up important personal and family obligations for work.
  • Employers should not set incentives that push staff to break the Standards.
Loyal to the employer, but never at the expense of clients, markets, or the Code.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis4/55
Guidance

Leaving an employer: prepare, do not poach

You may prepare to compete while still employed: write a business plan, rent an office, register a company, look for a job. Preparation must not breach your duty to the current employer.

Before you leave, you must not:

  • solicit the employer's clients or staff to follow you;
  • take client lists, records, models or other property;
  • misuse confidential information or divert business to yourself.

After leaving, you may contact former clients using public sources, unless an agreement such as a non-compete forbids it.

Preparing to compete is allowed; soliciting before you leave is not.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis5/55
Guidance

Client lists, records and non-competes

  • Records belong to the employer: client lists, files, models, research, emails, even copies on your own phone. Take none without permission.
  • Simply knowing the names of former clients is generally not confidential, unless an agreement or the law says it is.
  • Non-compete agreements: know what you signed and abide by it. Ask a lawyer if unsure.
  • Social media: follow the firm's policy. Accounts and contacts used for firm business may belong to the firm, and must not be used to solicit clients before you leave.
The firm owns the records; you own your experience.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis6/55
Guidance

Whistleblowing

Your duty to the employer ranks below your duty to clients and to the integrity of markets.

  • If the employer is engaged in illegal or unethical activity, acts that would normally breach loyalty can be justified: refusing instructions, breaking an internal policy, or copying records to preserve evidence.
  • This is allowed only when the intent is clearly to protect clients or the market, not for personal gain.
  • Usual first step: raise it with supervisors or compliance; go outside when that fails or is unsafe.
Whistleblowing to protect clients or markets is not disloyalty; doing it for personal gain is.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis7/55
Guidance

Independent practice and the nature of employment

  • Independent practice means doing work for pay outside your job that could compete with your employer, such as advising clients privately. Before starting, tell the employer the type of services, expected duration and compensation, and wait for consent.
  • Nature of employment: are you an employee or an independent contractor? It turns on control: who sets your hours, place and tools, pays expenses, and whether you work for others. A contractor's duties follow the agreement, so define the scope clearly. When unsure, take the conservative view.
Get consent before competing on the side; know whether you are an employee or a contractor.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis8/55
Recommended procedures

IV(A): how to comply

The handbook suggests firms have, and staff understand:

  • Competition policy: what outside work is restricted.
  • Termination policy: how departures work, including records, devices and client contact.
  • Incident reporting: how to raise suspected wrongdoing safely.
  • Employee classification: employee or contractor, and what each owes.
  • A social media policy covering business accounts and contacts.

For members: read these, follow them, and ask before you act.

Know the firm's rules on competing, leaving and reporting before you need them.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis9/55
Case

Case: the farewell email that came too early

Chintu accepts the rival's offer. Three weeks before resigning, he emails 40 of his firm's clients from a list he exported: "I am moving to Lotus AMC next month. Please move your accounts with me." Did Chintu most likely violate IV(A)?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation. He solicited the employer's clients while still employed, and he used the firm's client list. Both breach the duty of loyalty. He could have prepared quietly, resigned, and then contacted former clients using public information.

No soliciting the employer's clients until you have left, and never with its records.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis10/55
Case

Case: preparing, then competing

Ravi, a charterholder at Sharma ji's firm, registers his own advisory company and rents an office while still employed. He contacts no clients and takes no records. He has no non-compete. After resigning, he calls former clients using numbers from a public directory. Violation of IV(A)?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. Preparing to compete is allowed if it does not harm the employer. He solicited only after leaving, used public information rather than firm records, and no agreement barred him.

Plan while employed, compete after leaving, and use only public information.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis11/55
Exam trap

IV(A) traps

  • Preparing to compete (plans, office, company) is fine. Soliciting clients before you leave is not.
  • Client lists, models and files you built at work belong to the employer.
  • Knowing former clients' names is not confidential, absent an agreement or law; using the firm's records is the breach.
  • Whistleblowing to protect clients or markets is not disloyalty.
  • Side work that competes needs the employer's consent first.
  • Pinky is not a member or candidate, so the Standards do not bind her. Chintu is a candidate, so they bind him.
Ask: did they act against the employer while still paid by it, or take what the employer owns?
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis12/55
The Standard

IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements

In plain words: do not accept gifts, benefits, compensation or consideration that compete with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict with, your employer's interest, unless you obtain written consent from all parties involved.

Why: extra money from someone else can pull your judgment away from the employer's clients and business. The employer has a right to know, and to say no.

Written consent includes an email. Get it before you accept.

Outside pay or perks that could conflict: written consent from all parties, before accepting.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis13/55
Guidance

What needs written consent

ArrangementRule
Client offers a bonus for future performanceIV(B): written consent from employer (and the client) before accepting
Paid board seat, outside consultingIV(B): written consent first
Client's gift for past serviceLower risk to independence; disclose it to the employer
Unpaid, unrelated hobby workNo conflict: IV(B) not triggered

The test is conflict or competition with the employer, not the size of the gift.

Pay tied to future performance from someone other than your employer needs written consent.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis14/55
Recommended procedures

IV(B): how to comply

  • Make an immediate written report to your employer about any proposed compensation beyond what the employer pays.
  • State the terms: the nature of the compensation, the approximate amount, and the duration.
  • Wait for written consent from all parties before accepting.
  • Firms: have a clear process for outside activities and keep the approvals on file.
Report nature, amount and duration in writing; accept only after written consent.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis15/55
Case

Case: the Goa bonus

A wealthy client tells Chintu: "Beat the Nifty this year and I will pay for a week in Goa for you and your family." Chintu says yes and tells no one at the firm. He beats the index and takes the trip. Did Chintu most likely violate the Standards?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation of IV(B). A reward from a client for future performance could make Chintu favour that client over others, a conflict with the employer's interest. He needed written consent from his employer before accepting.

A client's reward for future results needs the employer's written consent first.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis16/55
Case

Case: the board seat

Sharma ji is invited to join the board of Chai & Co, an unlisted tea chain, for Rs 4 lakh a year. His firm does not invest in it. Before accepting, he sends the CEO a written description: role, fee and term. The CEO approves by email. He accepts. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. He reported the nature, amount and duration in writing and received written consent before accepting. An email counts as written consent.

Written report first, written consent next, then accept.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis17/55
Exam trap

IV(B) traps

  • Verbal permission is not enough: consent must be written (email is fine).
  • Consent must come before accepting, not after the trip.
  • "From all parties involved": usually the employer, and the client offering the arrangement.
  • Telling the client is not the same as getting the employer's consent.
  • The trigger is a possible conflict or competition, not the amount.
In IV(B) answers, look for the words written, before, and employer.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis18/55
The Standard

IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors

In plain words: make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to your supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards.

  • "Anyone" includes staff who are not CFA members or candidates.
  • Reasonable efforts mean an adequate compliance system, used: rules, training, monitoring, and action when something goes wrong.
  • You are not guaranteeing that no one ever breaks a rule. You are responsible for reasonable prevention and detection.
Supervisors must make reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations by everyone they supervise.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis19/55
Guidance

Adequate procedures, and what to do when they fail

  • Inadequate procedures: if the firm's compliance system cannot reasonably prevent and detect violations, decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until it adopts adequate procedures.
  • When a violation surfaces: respond promptly, investigate the extent, and take steps so it does not recur, such as limiting the person's activities or increasing monitoring. Taking their word for it is not enough; nor is just reporting it upward.
  • Delegation: you may delegate supervisory tasks, but you keep the supervisory responsibility.
No adequate system: decline in writing. Violation found: investigate and act. Delegating never removes the duty.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis20/55
Recommended procedures

IV(C): an adequate compliance system

Compliance procedures should:

  • be written, clear and easy to understand;
  • name a compliance officer with real authority;
  • set out the chain of supervision and each person's duties;
  • describe how monitoring is done and documented;
  • say how violations are reported and punished.

Supervisors should also: urge the firm to adopt a code of ethics, distribute the procedures, train staff, review them regularly, and act on breaches.

An adequate system is written, owned, monitored, enforced and taught.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis21/55
Case

Case: the gentle warning

Compliance flags that Pinky, a trader Sharma ji supervises, buys stocks for her own account minutes before large client orders. Sharma ji tells her, "Don't do it again, okay?" He does not investigate further or change any monitoring. Pinky is not a CFA member. Who most likely violated the Standards?

Verdict (tap to see)

Sharma ji violated IV(C). Learning of a likely violation, he had to investigate promptly and take steps such as restricting her trading and increasing monitoring. A verbal warning is not reasonable supervision. Pinky is not bound by the Standards (she may have broken the law and firm rules), but her supervisor is.

Supervisors who learn of misconduct must investigate and act, not just warn.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis22/55
Case

Case: a violation despite good supervision

Sharma ji's team has written procedures, training and regular monitoring. Despite them, a junior analyst secretly breaks the personal trading rules. Monitoring catches it within a week. Sharma ji investigates that day, restricts the analyst's trading and increases monitoring. Did Sharma ji violate IV(C)?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. IV(C) requires reasonable efforts, not perfection. Adequate procedures existed, they detected the problem, and he responded promptly and firmly.

A violation under you is not your violation if you had a reasonable system and acted on it.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis23/55
Exam trap

IV(C) traps

  • Delegating tasks does not delegate responsibility.
  • Supervision covers non-members too, even though the Standards themselves do not bind those staff.
  • A violation by a subordinate does not prove the supervisor violated IV(C). Check: adequate procedures, and a prompt response?
  • Inadequate procedures: decline supervision in writing, do not just "do your best".
  • Relying on the employee's promise, or only reporting upward, is not enough.
IV(C) asks two things: was there a reasonable system, and did the supervisor act when it fired?
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis24/55
The Standard

V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis

In plain words, two duties:

  1. Exercise diligence, independence and thoroughness when you analyse investments, make recommendations and take investment actions.
  2. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for every analysis, recommendation or action.

How much work is enough depends on the investment and your role. A complex structured product needs more digging than a large, well-covered stock. Research can be your own, the firm's, or a third party's.

Do the homework the decision deserves, and be able to show it.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis25/55
Guidance

Using third-party research

You may rely on research from others (brokers, data vendors, a colleague) if you made reasonable efforts to confirm it has a sound basis. Check:

  • the assumptions used;
  • the rigour of the analysis;
  • whether it is timely;
  • whether it is objective and independent.

Review research providers periodically. If you have reason to doubt a report, you may not lean on it.

Third-party research is usable only after you have checked it is sound.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis26/55
Guidance

Quantitative models, external advisers

  • Quant models: understand the assumptions and limits of the models you use or build. Test them across a range of scenarios, including extreme ones, not only normal markets. A housing model that assumes prices never fall has no reasonable basis.
  • External advisers and sub-advisers: before hiring, and regularly after, review their investment process, adherence to stated strategy, compliance and internal controls, quality of returns, and operations.
A model is only as reasonable as the worst scenario you tested it on.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis27/55
Guidance

Group research decisions

Many recommendations come from a committee. What if you disagree?

  • You may document your dissent.
  • If you believe the process was sound, and the consensus has a reasonable and adequate basis and is independent and objective, you need not remove your name from the report.
  • If the process itself lacked a reasonable basis, that is a different problem: raise it, and do not put your name to it.
Disagreeing with a sound group decision does not require you to disassociate from it.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis28/55
Recommended procedures

V(A): how to comply

Firms should:

  • require that research reports, credit ratings and recommendations have a basis that can be shown to be reasonable and adequate;
  • give analysts detailed written guidance on proper research and supervision;
  • set measurable criteria for judging third-party research and providers;
  • write guidance for testing quantitative models, including stress scenarios;
  • set criteria and review procedures for external advisers;
  • document how group research decisions are made.
Firms make diligence routine: written standards, criteria, tests and records.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis29/55
Case

Case: copy, paste, publish

Short of time, Chintu copies a broker's buy recommendation on Kaveri Cement into his own report. He does not check its assumptions. The broker's model still uses 2023 cement prices, before a sharp cost increase. Did Chintu most likely violate V(A)?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation. He relied on third-party research without assessing its assumptions or timeliness, so his recommendation lacked a reasonable and adequate basis. Being busy is not an exception.

Borrowed research must be checked before it becomes your recommendation.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis30/55
Case

Case: outvoted, still named

The research committee reviews a full model, management meetings and scenario tests, then votes 4 to 1 to rate Monsoon Motors a buy. Chintu thinks the valuation is rich and his dissent is minuted. The report goes out with Chintu listed on the team. He believes the process was thorough. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. The group process was sound and the consensus had a reasonable and adequate basis. Chintu may record his dissent without removing his name.

A minority view on a sound process is recorded, not a reason to quit the report.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis31/55
Exam trap

V(A) traps

  • A famous source is not a reasonable basis. Check assumptions, rigour, timeliness, objectivity.
  • Dissenting from a sound group decision does not require removing your name.
  • Model tests must include extreme scenarios, not only normal markets.
  • Due diligence on external advisers continues after hiring them.
  • The required depth of research varies with the product and your role.
V(A) answers turn on one question: was there a reasonable and adequate basis?
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis32/55
The Standard

V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients

In plain words, four duties to clients and prospects:

  1. Disclose the basic format and general principles of the investment process you use to analyse investments, select securities and build portfolios, and promptly disclose changes that might materially affect it.
  2. Disclose significant limitations and risks of the investment process.
  3. Use reasonable judgment to identify the important factors and include them in your communications.
  4. Distinguish between fact and opinion in your analysis and recommendations.
Tell clients how you invest, what can go wrong, what matters, and which bits are opinion.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis33/55
Guidance

Process changes, risks and short formats

  • Process changes: switching from fundamental research to a quant model, adding a new data source, or hiring a sub-adviser are changes clients must hear about promptly.
  • Risks and limits: for example leverage, derivatives, liquidity, counterparty risk, and model limits. You need not predict every outcome, only disclose the significant risks.
  • Short formats (social posts, text messages) cannot say everything. Point clients to the fuller report with the details.
  • Keep records of what you communicated.
Short messages are fine if the full story, risks included, is one click away.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis34/55
Guidance

Fact or opinion?

Cover the right column, then check yourself:

StatementLabel
"Kaveri's revenue grew 12% last year."Fact
"EPS will be Rs 50 next year."Opinion (a forecast)
"The dividend yield is 2%."Fact (today)
"The stock is cheap."Opinion
"The bond will never default."Opinion, and a dangerous one

Writing a forecast as if it were certain ("will be", "never") is a V(B) violation. Say "we estimate", "we expect", "in our opinion".

Forecasts are opinions; present them as estimates, never as facts.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis35/55
Recommended procedures

V(B): how to comply

In research and client reports, include the basics:

  • a summary of the investment process and how securities were selected;
  • the key factors, assumptions and expected time frame;
  • the significant risks and limitations;
  • clear labels on opinions and estimates.

Then: tell clients promptly about material process changes, and keep records of the communications.

Process, factors, risks, labels, and a record of what you said.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis36/55
Case

Case: the silent switch

Sharma ji's flagship fund has always picked stocks by fundamental research. In 2026 he quietly moves the whole fund to a quantitative model bought from a vendor, which trades far more often. The marketing material and client letters still describe fundamental stock picking. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation of V(B). A material change to the investment process must be promptly disclosed to clients and prospects, along with the new process's significant risks and limits. (Using a model without understanding it also raises V(A).)

Change the process, tell the clients, promptly.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis37/55
Case

Case: the short post

Chintu posts on social media: "Monsoon Motors: BUY, our 12-month target Rs 640 (estimate). Full report and risks: link." The linked report explains the process, assumptions and main risks, and was sent to all clients at the same time. Violation of V(B)?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. The target is labelled as an estimate, and the short format points to a full report with the process and risks.

A brief message is fine when it labels opinions and points to the full report.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis38/55
Exam trap

V(B) traps

  • Forecasts and price targets are opinions. Presenting them as facts is a violation.
  • Material changes to the process (new model, new data, new sub-adviser) must be disclosed promptly.
  • You must disclose significant risks, not every conceivable one.
  • Short formats are fine with a pointer to full information.
  • V(B) covers prospective clients too.
In V(B) questions, hunt for a hidden change, a hidden risk, or an opinion dressed as fact.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis39/55
The Standard

V(C) Record Retention

In plain words: develop and maintain appropriate records to support your investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospects.

  • Records include models, spreadsheets, notes from company meetings, emails, research, data used, and social media communications.
  • Records belong to the firm, not to you.
  • Local law or regulation sets how long to keep them. Where no requirement applies, the Standards recommend at least seven years.
Keep the evidence behind every recommendation; it belongs to the firm; seven years if no rule says otherwise.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis40/55
Recommended procedures

V(C): how to comply

  • The firm usually owns the retention system. Members should follow it, and make sure their own work is captured.
  • Follow local regulatory retention periods; with none, keep records at least seven years.
  • Include electronic and social media records.
  • When you change firms, leave the records behind. At the new firm, recreate the support for any recommendation from public information or the company itself, not from memory or the old firm's files.
New firm, new records: rebuild the support from public sources.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis41/55
Case

Case: the USB drive

On his last day, Chintu copies his cement sector models and company meeting notes to a USB drive. "I built them," he says. At Lotus AMC he uses them to support his first report. Did Chintu most likely violate the Standards?

Verdict (tap to see)

Violation. The models and notes are the old firm's records (V(C)) and taking them breaches loyalty (IV(A)). His new report rests on records he had no right to use.

Work you built at a firm is the firm's record; it stays when you leave.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis42/55
Case

Case: rebuilding the file

Ravi joins a new firm and wants to keep covering cement stocks. He takes nothing from his old firm. He rebuilds his models from annual reports, exchange filings and industry data, holds fresh meetings with company management, and files all of it before publishing. Violation?

Verdict (tap to see)

No violation. He recreated the support from public information and the companies themselves, and kept records at the new firm. His experience and skill go with him; the old firm's records do not.

Your skills move with you; your records must be rebuilt.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis43/55
Exam trap

V(C) traps

  • Records belong to the firm, even ones you created.
  • Seven years is the Standards' recommendation only when no regulation applies. Local rules come first.
  • Memory is not a record. Rebuild support from public sources at a new firm.
  • Emails, chats and social media posts are records too.
  • Taking files when leaving is a V(C) and IV(A) problem at once.
No regulation: seven years. Leaving: records stay. New firm: rebuild.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis44/55
Sharma ji's red pen

7 things to remember

  1. IV(A): prepare to compete, but no soliciting or records before you leave.
  2. Whistleblowing for clients or markets is allowed; for personal gain, no.
  3. IV(B): conflicting outside pay needs written consent from all parties, first.
  4. IV(C): reasonable system plus prompt action. Inadequate system: decline in writing.
  5. V(A): check third-party research; stress-test models; dissent need not mean leaving the report.
  6. V(B): disclose process, changes and risks; label opinions.
  7. V(C): records are the firm's; seven years if no rule; rebuild at a new firm.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the back of a resignation letter.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis45/55
Exam question 1 of 10

Rohan, a charterholder, plans to start his own advisory firm. Before resigning, which action most likely violates IV(A) Loyalty?

  1. A. Renting an office and registering his new company.
  2. B. Phoning his employer's clients to ask them to move with him.
  3. C. Telling his employer he is resigning in two weeks.
Show answer

Answer: B. Soliciting the employer's clients while still employed breaches the duty of loyalty. A is permitted preparation that does not harm the employer. C is ordinary notice and harms no one.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis46/55
Exam question 2 of 10

An analyst wants to prepare tax returns for private clients for a fee on weekends, which competes with a service her employer sells. Under IV(A), she should most likely:

  1. A. tell her employer the type of services, expected duration and pay, and start only after consent.
  2. B. go ahead, because the work is outside office hours.
  3. C. tell the private clients about her employer, but not her employer about the clients.
Show answer

Answer: A. Independent practice that competes with the employer needs notice of the services, duration and compensation, and the employer's consent before starting. B is wrong: competition does not depend on the hour. C reverses who must be told.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis47/55
Exam question 3 of 10

Which action is least likely to violate IV(A) Loyalty?

  1. A. Taking the client list to a new employer.
  2. B. Using the old firm's valuation model at a new job.
  3. C. Copying employer records to give a regulator evidence of fraud against clients, with no personal gain.
Show answer

Answer: C. Acts that normally breach loyalty can be justified when the clear intent is to protect clients or market integrity, not personal gain. A and B take the employer's property, which breaches loyalty (and V(C) for records).

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis48/55
Exam question 4 of 10

A client offers an analyst a bonus if the client's portfolio beats its benchmark this year. To comply with IV(B), the analyst must:

  1. A. tell the client that the bonus will be shared with the team.
  2. B. get written consent from her employer before accepting.
  3. C. decline, because all outside compensation is banned.
Show answer

Answer: B. IV(B) allows such arrangements only with written consent from all parties involved, obtained before accepting. A does not involve the employer at all. C overstates the rule: consent, not a ban, is required.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis49/55
Exam question 5 of 10

A supervisor learns that a trader he supervises may have front-run client orders. Which response best meets IV(C)?

  1. A. Report it to his own manager and accept the trader's promise not to repeat it.
  2. B. Fire the trader at once without looking into the facts.
  3. C. Promptly investigate, restrict the trader's activities and increase monitoring.
Show answer

Answer: C. IV(C) requires a prompt investigation and steps to stop recurrence, such as limits and closer monitoring. A relies on reporting upward and a promise, which is not enough. B skips the investigation and does not test whether the firm's procedures need fixing.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis50/55
Exam question 6 of 10

A newly hired head of trading, a charterholder, finds that her firm has no written compliance procedures for trading staff. She should most likely:

  1. A. decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until adequate procedures are adopted.
  2. B. accept the role and supervise as best she can.
  3. C. accept the role, since the firm, not she, is responsible for procedures.
Show answer

Answer: A. With inadequate procedures she cannot make reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations, so she should decline supervisory responsibility in writing until adequate procedures exist. B and C leave her exposed under IV(C).

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis51/55
Exam question 7 of 10

An analyst on a research committee disagrees with its buy rating. The committee's process was thorough and its conclusion has a reasonable basis. Under V(A), she:

  1. A. must have her name removed from the report.
  2. B. may document her dissent and remain named on the report.
  3. C. must publish her own contrary report to clients.
Show answer

Answer: B. When the group process is sound and the consensus has a reasonable and adequate basis, a dissenting member need not disassociate. A is not required. C could confuse clients and is not required by the Standards.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis52/55
Exam question 8 of 10

Which practice best meets V(A) for a firm's quantitative risk model?

  1. A. Understanding its assumptions and testing it under extreme as well as normal scenarios.
  2. B. Testing it on the last three calm years of data, which match current conditions.
  3. C. Relying on the vendor's assurance that the model is accurate.
Show answer

Answer: A. V(A) expects users to understand a model's assumptions and limits and to test it across scenarios, including stress. B ignores extreme outcomes. C replaces diligence with trust.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis53/55
Exam question 9 of 10

Which action most likely violates V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients?

  1. A. A short social post with a buy rating, an estimated target, and a link to the full report.
  2. B. Switching a fund to a new quant model without telling its clients.
  3. C. Labelling an earnings forecast as "our estimate" in a report.
Show answer

Answer: B. A material change to the investment process must be disclosed promptly. A is fine: brief formats can point to full information. C correctly separates opinion from fact.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 6: Standards IV and V: Duties to Employers and Investment Analysis54/55
Exam question 10 of 10

Where no regulatory requirement applies, the Standards recommend keeping records that support investment recommendations for at least:

  1. A. three years.
  2. B. five years.
  3. C. seven years.
Show answer

Answer: C. The recommended minimum is seven years where no regulatory requirement applies; local regulations take precedence when they exist. A and B are shorter than the Standards' recommendation.

Loyal, careful, documented

Chintu resigned on Monday, took nothing but his skills, and told no client until he had left. At the new desk he rebuilt his cement models from annual reports. Sharma ji sent a one-line email: "Good. Data dikhao, always." Chintu framed it.
