Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate1/63
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • CFA Institute: runs the CFA Program and owns the Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct.
  • Member: a CFA Institute member; charterholders are members allowed to use the CFA designation.
  • IPO: initial public offering: a company's first sale of shares to the public.
  • IPS: investment policy statement: a client's written objectives and limits.
  • Underwriter: the investment bank that sells a company's new securities for a fee.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate2/63
Story

Two hats, one head

Chintu, a Level I candidate at a Mumbai investment firm, writes a glowing report on Maha Cement. Sharma ji, the CIO and a CFA charterholder, spots Chintu's name in the shareholder list.

Is Chintu a crook? Not necessarily. Owning a stock you cover is common and often legal. The problem is that clients reading the report cannot judge his bias if they do not know.

Standard VI is about exactly this: conflicts of interest. Standard VII is about how members and candidates behave toward CFA Institute and its exam, and how they describe the charter.

A conflict is not a crime by itself; hiding it, or letting it hurt clients, is the violation.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate3/63
Map

Five sub-standards in this chapter

StandardOne-line meaning
VI(A) Avoid or Disclose ConflictsAvoid conflicts, or disclose them fully, prominently, in plain words
VI(B) Priority of TransactionsClients first, employer second, your own account last
VI(C) Referral FeesDisclose any benefit paid or received for a referral
VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute ProgramsNo cheating, no leaking exam content
VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA ProgramNo exaggerating what the charter or candidacy means
Standard VI is titled Conflicts of Interest; Standard VII is Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate4/63
VI(A), the Standard

VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts, in plain words

Members and candidates must avoid, or make full and fair disclosure of, every matter that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity, or interfere with their duties to clients, prospective clients and the employer.

Disclosures must be prominent, in plain language, and actually communicate the point.

New in 2024: the Standard now says avoid first. Older material calls it "Disclosure of Conflicts" and only required disclosure. Today: avoid the conflict when you reasonably can; when you cannot, disclose it fully and clearly.

VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts: avoid the conflict if reasonable; if not, disclose it clearly to everyone it could affect.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate5/63
VI(A), guidance 1

Where conflicts come from

A conflict of interest is anything that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity, or make people ask whether your judgement is free from bias.

  • Stock ownership in companies you recommend or clients hold: the most common one.
  • Directorships and consultancies with an issuer.
  • Compensation: bonuses that reward short-term results, commissions, payments from issuers.
  • Firm ties: investment banking, underwriting, market making, fund fee rebates, unusual fee or subadvisory deals.
Ownership, board seats, pay structures and banking relationships are the classic conflicts to avoid or disclose.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate6/63
VI(A), guidance 2

Telling your employer

The same things you would tell clients must also be reported to the employer promptly: stock you own in covered companies, outside board seats, and financial or other pressures on your decisions.

Give enough detail for the employer to judge the impact and decide how to resolve it.

Employers may ban some activities outright (personal trading in covered stocks, outside boards) to avoid even the appearance of a conflict. Members must follow those rules.

A conflict with the employer's own business, one that could stop you giving full commitment to the job, should be avoided, or else reported.

Employers need the same conflict information as clients, early enough to act on it.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate7/63
VI(A), guidance 3

Telling clients, and the board seat problem

Always avoid or disclose to clients any relationship between an issuer and you or your firm: directorship, consultancy, underwriting, market making, material beneficial ownership.

Take reasonable steps to find your firm's conflicts too, such as fee rebates from fund houses, and disclose them.

A member who serves as a director faces three conflicts (right panel). The fix: keep the director behind a firewall, away from the people making investment decisions.

Beneficial ownership is about economic interest or control, not whose name is on the share certificate.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate8/63
VI(A), guidance 4

Prominent, plain, and kept up to date

Prominent means placed where the reader will see it: not in tiny font, not hidden in a footnote or appendix. Plain language means common words, no jargon.

You decide how often and how to disclose, but err on the side of caution.

Best practice: update the disclosure when a conflict changes materially. Example: the firm switches bonuses from annual profits to quarterly profits, which raises the pressure for short-term results.

Also try to mitigate the conflict and tell people how you did it.

A disclosure nobody can find or understand is not full and fair disclosure.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate9/63
VI(A), decision path

Avoid or disclose? Run the flowchart

Run the chart in this order:

  1. Could the matter reasonably be expected to affect your objectivity or your duties? If not, there is nothing to disclose.
  2. If yes, can you reasonably avoid it? Sell the shares, decline the board seat, hand the report to a colleague.
  3. If you cannot, disclose it to everyone affected, prominently and in plain words. Then mitigate it and update the disclosure if it changes.
Order of preference: avoid, then disclose and mitigate. Silence is never an option.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate10/63
VI(A), compliance

What good practice looks like

WhoPractice
MemberAvoid where reasonable; otherwise disclose, mitigate, and update when the conflict changes
MemberReport ownership, board seats and outside pressures to the employer promptly
MemberAsk to hand off coverage when a personal stake is large
FirmRestrict personal trading and outside boards; firewall directors from investment decisions
FirmDisclose firm conflicts: banking ties, market making, fee rebates, pay incentives
The member owns the disclosure; the firm builds walls and rules that make conflicts rarer.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate11/63
Case: VI(A)

The inherited cement shares

Sharma ji has rated Maha Cement a buy for a year. His wife then inherits Rs 3 crore of Maha shares. His employer asks him for a follow-up report. He writes it, keeps the buy rating (he honestly still likes the stock), and mentions the inheritance to nobody.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(A). His wife's holding makes him a beneficial owner through his immediate family, and it could reasonably affect his objectivity. At minimum he must tell his employer and disclose the holding in the report. Best practice: ask for another analyst to write it. His honest belief in the rating does not cure the missing disclosure.

Family holdings count. Disclose them to the employer and in the report, or hand the report to someone else.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate12/63
Case: VI(A)

Quarterly bonus, long-term clients

Mehra, a CFA charterholder, runs long-horizon pension accounts. Her firm introduces a bonus based on quarterly performance against peers. To win it, she fills the accounts with high-beta stocks that sit uneasily with the clients' IPS. She tells clients nothing about the new bonus and recommends no change to their objectives.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(A). The new pay plan conflicts with the clients' long-term objectives, so she had to disclose it. Firms may pay for performance, but short-term pressure cannot override actions consistent with the IPS.

A pay structure that pulls against client objectives is a conflict to disclose.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate13/63
Case: VI(A)

The banker's research, done right

Chintu's firm underwrote Ganga Bank's latest bond issue and hopes to win its next deal. Chintu writes a report on Ganga Bank. The first page says, in normal type: "Our firm was underwriter for Ganga Bank's 2026 bond issue and may seek more business from it." His employer already knows. His analysis is sound and his rating is his own.

Verdict (tap)

No violation. An investment banking relationship is a classic conflict, but here it is disclosed fully, prominently and in plain language, and the analysis stays independent. VI(A) does not ban the relationship; it bans hiding it.

A disclosed, prominent, plain-language conflict with independent analysis satisfies VI(A).
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate14/63
Case: VI(A)

Pinky's secret bonus

A promoter of Rocket Ltd pays Pinky, a trader, for every client she moves into Rocket shares. She tells neither her clients nor her employer. Pinky is not a CFA Institute member and not a candidate. Next month, Chintu, a Level I candidate, accepts the same deal.

Verdict (tap)

Pinky: no violation of the CFA Institute Standards, because they bind only members and candidates. She may still break the law and her firm's rules. Chintu: violation of VI(A), because he hid compensation that could bias his advice. Best practice was to refuse the offer. Candidates are bound from the day they enrol.

The Standards apply to members and candidates only; for them, secret pay for pushing a product is a VI(A) violation.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate15/63
Case: VI(A)

The CIO's old classmate

Sharma ji also advises a trust's retirement fund. His IIM classmate Nagle starts a real estate firm and asks for business. The fund's real estate returns had matched the benchmark. Sharma ji moves the whole allocation to Nagle's firm, partly to help a friend. The only trace is a new name in next year's list of external managers.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(A). He did not disclose the personal relationship to his employer. Telling them would let them judge whether friendship impaired his independence in switching managers. The friend's firm may even do well; that does not fix the missing disclosure.

Personal relationships that could sway a decision must be disclosed, even if the outcome turns out fine.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate16/63
Exam trap

VI(A) traps examiners love

  • Owning shares is not banned; failing to disclose them is the violation. A firm may still ban it by policy.
  • Footnotes and appendices are not prominent disclosure.
  • Disclosure goes to clients, prospects and the employer. Telling only one group is incomplete.
  • Family holdings make you a beneficial owner.
  • Disclosure does not make an unsuitable trade suitable; that is a separate duty.
  • "Best practice" in an answer (decline, reassign) is better than the minimum (disclose), but the minimum is what avoids a violation.
Ask three things: was it a real conflict, was it avoided or disclosed, and was the disclosure prominent and complete?
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate17/63
VI(B), the Standard

VI(B) Priority of Transactions, in plain words

Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over transactions in which the member or candidate is the beneficial owner.

Beneficial owner: you ultimately own, control, can direct, or have a material interest in the investment. That covers your own account, your immediate family's accounts and any account in which you have a direct or indirect financial interest.

You must not benefit from, or pass on, knowledge of pending client trades. Clients and the employer get an adequate chance to act on a recommendation before you do.

Clients first, employer next, your own beneficially owned accounts last.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate18/63
VI(B), timeline

Who trades when: the queue on a clock

Follow one recommendation through the day:

  1. The research team approves a buy rating on Maha Cement.
  2. The report goes out and clients get a fair chance to trade on it.
  3. The firm's own account trades only after clients.
  4. Chintu, who knew the rating was coming, waits out the blackout period, gets pre-clearance, and only then buys for himself.

Buying before step 2 is front-running: trading ahead of clients on what you know about their coming orders.

Personal trades wait until clients, and then the employer, have had an adequate opportunity to act.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate19/63
VI(B), guidance 1

Personal investing is allowed

Nothing is unethical about investment professionals making money from their own investments, as long as:

  1. the client is not disadvantaged by the trade,
  2. the member does not benefit personally from trades made for clients, and
  3. the member follows applicable regulations (and the firm's policies).

Holding the same positions as clients is not automatically a conflict; some clients want aligned interests. You may even sell against your own recommendation for genuine personal reasons, such as paying for a wedding or a flat.

VI(B) does not ban personal trading; it bans personal trading that puts you ahead of clients or the employer.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate20/63
VI(B), guidance 2

Family accounts: same queue, same place

A family member's account that is a client account is treated like any other client account. It must not get special treatment, and it must not be disadvantaged either.

So if Chintu's mother pays the firm fees and a suitable IPO comes along, she gets her fair share alongside other suitable clients. Putting her last "to look clean" breaches his duty to her as a client.

If Chintu is a beneficial owner of that account, the firm may still require him to pre-clear and report its trades.

Family client accounts are neither favoured nor penalised; they join the normal allocation.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate21/63
VI(B), guidance 3

IPOs and private placements

Equity IPOs: hot issues are scarce. If you take shares personally, it can look like you took an attractive opportunity away from clients, or that someone handed it to you as an incentive for future business. The cleanest fix: don't participate. If firm policy allows it, pre-clear every IPO purchase, even when there seems to be no conflict.

Private placements (shares sold privately to a few chosen investors): firms may limit them strictly. Avoid any deal that could look like a favour or gift meant to influence future judgement or reward past business.

Hot IPOs and private placements: abstain if you can, pre-clear if your firm allows them.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate22/63
VI(B), guidance 4

Blackouts, reporting and pre-clearance

Common firm procedures that members must follow:

  • Blackout or restricted periods: people involved in investment decisions may not trade around client trades, which blocks front-running.
  • Disclosure of holdings you beneficially own, when you join and periodically after.
  • Duplicate confirmations: your broker sends copies of your trades and statements to the firm. It signals independent checking and shows the flow of trades, not just holdings.
  • Pre-clearance of planned personal trades, to catch conflicts before they happen.
Blackouts stop front-running; holdings reports, duplicate confirms and pre-clearance let the firm check.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate23/63
VI(B), compliance

Recommended procedures, in one table

ProcedurePurpose
Limit IPO participation; pre-clearNo taking scarce deals from clients
Restrict private placementsNo favours that buy judgement
Blackout periodsStop front-running
Holdings reports, duplicate confirms, pre-clearanceLet the firm verify
Disclose the policy to clients on requestReal detail, not boilerplate

"Staff are subject to trading policies" is boilerplate. A useful disclosure says what the rules actually are.

Members must follow the employer's personal trading rules and should be able to explain them to clients.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate24/63
Case: VI(B)

Chintu jumps the queue

Chintu finds that Vayu Airlines is cheap. Instead of sending his buy recommendation to the investment committee now, he sits on it for a week while he buys shares in his own account. Then he submits the report, the committee approves it, and the firm's clients buy.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(B). He used his knowledge of the stock's value for himself before his employer and its clients could benefit. The order is clients, then employer, then Chintu. Being a Level I candidate gives no exemption.

Delaying a recommendation so you can trade first is a textbook VI(B) violation.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate25/63
Case: VI(B)

Mummy gets the leftovers

Rao, a CFA charterholder and portfolio manager, runs her parents' retirement account, which pays the firm normal fees. Whenever a suitable IPO arrives, she allocates to every other client first and gives her parents only what is left, "so nobody can say I favour family".

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(B). Her parents are fee-paying clients and deserve equal treatment. Disadvantaging them because they are family breaches her duty to them. If she is a beneficial owner of the account, she may also need to pre-clear and report its trades.

Bending over backwards against family is still unequal treatment.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate26/63
Case: VI(B)

Selling for a wedding

Sharma ji's firm rates Maha Cement a buy. He needs cash for his daughter's wedding and sells his own Maha shares. No client orders in Maha are pending, there is no blackout, and he pre-clears the trade under firm policy.

Verdict (tap)

No violation. A member may act against current advice for genuine personal financial reasons. Clients are not disadvantaged, he gains nothing from client trades, and he followed the firm's procedures.

Selling against your own rating for personal reasons is allowed if clients are not harmed and firm rules are followed.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate27/63
Case: VI(B)

Seven minutes after the call

At 10:00 an analyst tells the firm's branches in an internal video call that Suraksha Insurance is a sell. The written report reaches clients the next day. At 10:07, Dutta, a CFA charterholder who heads trading, closes the firm's long calls in Suraksha and buys puts. He says he was "preparing for client selling".

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(B). The firm's own account traded before clients had any chance to receive and act on the recommendation, which may have moved option prices against them. He should have waited until clients had the report and time to use it.

The firm's account also waits behind clients; trading on a call before clients see it breaks VI(B).
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate28/63
Exam trap

VI(B) traps examiners love

  • A spouse's or child's account is usually beneficially owned by you. Changing the name on the account changes nothing.
  • Family accounts that are clients are treated equally, not first and not last.
  • The employer's own account also comes after clients.
  • Personal trading is not banned; trading ahead of clients is.
  • Pre-clearing IPOs is recommended even with no apparent conflict.
  • Pinky is not a member or candidate, so she cannot violate the Standards, though her firm's rules still bind her.
Ask: who owns it economically, who traded first, and was everyone treated equally?
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate29/63
VI(C), the Standard

VI(C) Referral Fees, in plain words

Members and candidates must disclose to their employer, clients and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration or benefit received from or paid to others for recommending products or services.

Timing: before the client or prospect enters any formal agreement for services.

Content: the nature of the benefit and its estimated value.

Why: so clients can judge whether the recommendation is partial, and see the full cost of the service.

VI(C): disclose referral benefits in both directions, before the agreement, with nature and estimated value.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate30/63
VI(C), guidance

What counts, what to say, what firms do

QuestionAnswer
What counts?Any fee: cash, soft dollars (paid via client commissions) or in kind
Nature?Flat or %, one-time or ongoing, performance-based, research, other non-cash
Inside the firm?Yes: bonuses for internal referrals count
Firm practiceBan referral fees, or require approval
Member practiceReport referral income to the employer at least quarterly
Referral benefits include non-cash and internal ones; members in approved programmes update the employer at least quarterly.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate31/63
Case: VI(C)

The trust department's hidden bonus

Joshi, a CFA charterholder in a bank's trust department, gets Rs 5,000 from his own bank for every client he refers to the bank's wealth management desk who signs up. He refers several clients and never mentions the payment.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(C). The Standard makes no distinction between fees from outside parties and internal payments for steering business to another department. At the time of referral, he had to disclose the arrangement, including its nature and value.

Internal referral bonuses count as referral fees.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate32/63
Case: VI(C)

The consultant paid twice

A state pension plan hires Arora, a CFA charterholder, to pick an emerging markets manager. He recommends Overseas Investments, which is hired. A year later the plan learns that Arora charges managers a fee when his recommendation wins them a mandate. An independent review finds his choice was objective and suitable.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VI(C). He did not disclose the fee from Overseas. A good outcome does not cure non-disclosure, because the hidden payment implies a possible lack of objectivity.

A good recommendation does not excuse an undisclosed referral payment.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate33/63
Case: VI(C)

The CA uncle, done right

Chintu's firm has an approved arrangement: it pays a chartered accountant, Mr Iyer, a one-time Rs 10,000 for each client he refers. Before a new client signs, Chintu hands her a note in plain words stating the payment, that it is one-time, and its amount. His employer approved the programme and gets quarterly reports.

Verdict (tap)

No violation. The benefit paid is disclosed to the employer and to the prospect before any formal agreement, with its nature and value. That is exactly what VI(C) asks.

Paying or receiving referral fees is allowed when disclosed in time, with nature and value.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate34/63
Exam trap

VI(C) traps examiners love

  • Disclosure covers fees paid to others for sending you clients, not only fees you receive.
  • Before the formal agreement. Telling the client after signing is too late.
  • "We have referral arrangements" is not enough: state the nature and estimated value.
  • Free research, commission business and soft dollars are benefits too.
  • A good recommendation still violates VI(C) if the fee was hidden.
  • A hidden referral fee is also a conflict, but VI(C) is the Standard written for it, so it is usually the best answer.
Referral fee questions turn on three words: before, nature, value.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate35/63
VII(A), the Standard

VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs

Members and candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation, or the integrity, validity or security of CFA Institute programs.

Prohibited conduct includes:

  • cheating, giving or receiving help in an exam;
  • breaking exam rules and testing policies;
  • sharing confidential exam or program information;
  • getting around exam security;
  • improperly using an association with CFA Institute for personal or business gain;
  • misrepresenting information to CFA Institute.
VII(A) protects the exam and the CFA Institute name; it applies to members and candidates in any CFA Institute program.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate36/63
VII(A), guidance

After the exam: what you may say

AllowedNot allowed
How hard it felt; how you think you didSpecific questions, or details of them
Studying non-confidential material in a study groupBroad topics or formulas tested or not tested
Criticising CFA Institute's policies or feesWorking out answers to exam questions online
Saying you volunteer for CFA InstituteGraders or writers sharing questions, deliberations or scoring

All exam content stays confidential until CFA Institute itself releases it.

Feelings and opinions are fine; anything about what was or was not on the exam is confidential.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate37/63
VII(A), guidance 2

Opinions, volunteers and misusing the name

Opinions are free. Members and candidates may disagree with CFA Institute's policies, procedures or advocacy positions, publicly. They still may not reveal exam content while doing so.

Volunteers (question writers, graders, committee members) must not share confidential material: questions, deliberations, scoring information.

Misuse: using a CFA Institute role to gain business is a violation. A member may factually state that she serves on a committee, but must not imply that it gives her clients a special advantage.

Criticise all you like; just never leak confidential content or sell your CFA Institute role.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate38/63
VII(A), compliance

Staying safe as a candidate

WhenDo this
BeforeRead the CFA Program testing policies; breaking any of them is a VII(A) violation
Exam dayNo written material, no looking at other screens, cooperate with security
DeferralsTell the truth in any request to CFA Institute
AfterShare feelings, not content; ignore prep-provider requests for questions
AnytimeReport suspected leaks to CFA Institute
Every testing policy breach is a VII(A) breach, including lies on a deferral request.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate39/63
Case: VII(A)

Chintu's two posts

The evening after his Level I exam, Chintu posts twice in a candidates' group. Post 1: "Level I done! Brutal, but I think I passed. Biryani tonight!" Post 2: "So many FX questions. And not one on GIPS, so skip it next time."

Verdict (tap)

Post 1: no violation. Saying how hard it felt and how he thinks he did reveals no exam content. Post 2: violation of VII(A). Revealing which topics were heavily tested, and which were not tested at all, is confidential exam information and could help candidates still to sit the exam.

How you felt is yours to share; what was or was not on the exam is not.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate40/63
Case: VII(A)

The grader who talked

Sharma ji volunteers as a grader and agreed to discuss exam material only with CFA Institute staff and other graders. Weeks after grading ends, he tells Chintu and other candidates which question he graded, describes the guideline answer, and says few candidates scored well.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VII(A). He disclosed confidential information about a specific question and its scoring. The time that has passed does not matter: content stays confidential until CFA Institute releases it.

Volunteers carry the same confidentiality duty as candidates, and more.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate41/63
Case: VII(A)

The fee-hike rant

Chintu writes a sharp public blog post arguing that CFA Institute's exam fees are too high for Indian candidates and that its policies on deferrals are unfair. He mentions nothing about exam content.

Verdict (tap)

No violation. VII(A) does not cover expressing opinions about CFA Institute or its programs. Members and candidates are free to disagree publicly, as long as no confidential exam information is revealed.

Criticising CFA Institute is allowed; leaking its exam is not.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate42/63
Exam trap

VII(A) traps examiners love

  • Topics not tested are confidential too, not just questions.
  • Confidentiality has no expiry date until CFA Institute releases the material.
  • Answering a prep provider's survey with questions is a violation; employees who solicit them violate too if they are members or candidates.
  • A false deferral request violates VII(A) (and I(C) Misrepresentation).
  • Opinions about CFA Institute are not violations.
  • If Pinky is not a candidate she cannot violate the Standards, but a candidate who sells her questions can.
If it hints at exam content, cheats a rule, or trades on the CFA Institute name, it is VII(A).
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate43/63
VII(B), the Standard

VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

When referring to CFA Institute, membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, members and candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate what membership, the designation or candidacy means.

It covers every form of communication: business cards, letterhead, LinkedIn pages, email signatures, websites, CVs, ads and things said out loud.

Allowed: factual statements about the program's rigour and charterholders' commitment to ethics, and opinions stated as opinions. Not allowed: promising competence or performance because of the charter.

VII(B) is about honest labelling: no exaggeration of what the charter, membership or candidacy means.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate44/63
VII(B), guidance 1

Who may write CFA after their name

Earning the charter is not enough on its own. To keep using the designation, a charterholder must be a member in good standing, which each year means: completing the Membership Agreement, submitting the Professional Conduct Statement, and paying dues.

Miss any of these and membership lapses: no "CFA" on cards, emails or LinkedIn until reinstated. A former member may say "CFA charterholder, 2008 to 2020".

Retiring? CFA Institute has a retired status with lower dues; you must apply for it.

The right to use CFA after your name is renewed every year through the PCS, dues and the membership agreement.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate45/63
VII(B), guidance 2

How a candidate may describe candidacy

ProperImproper
Level I candidate in the CFA ProgramCFA Level I; CFA (Level I)
Passed Level II of the CFA ProgramCFA, Level II
Passed all three levels; eligible for the charter after the work experienceCFA, expected 2028; Charter pending

You are a candidate once accepted and enrolled for an exam, or while awaiting results. Skip enrolling and candidacy pauses until you enrol again.

No partial designation exists, and no expected charter date may be claimed: the award needs work experience and Board approval.

Say exactly what is true: candidate for, or passed, a level of the CFA Program. Never a partial CFA.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate46/63
VII(B), guidance 3

Using the mark: adjective, never noun

CFA Institute's trademark guide says the mark is an adjective, never a noun: "a CFA charterholder", not "a CFA". The quick test: drop "CFA" and the sentence should still make sense.

Write "Ravi Iyer, CFA" with a comma, and do not put the registered mark symbol after a person's name.

The mark must not be used in a company name, logo, product or website name such as "CFA Wealth". And never attach "CFA" to a pseudonym: "Expert, CFA" on an anonymous blog comment is a VII(B) violation.

CFA Institute trademark usage guide
CFA is an adjective (CFA charterholder), never a noun, a firm name or a tag on a pseudonym.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate47/63
VII(B), guidance 4

Facts and opinions yes, performance promises no

ProperImproper
The charter improved my skills (opinion)Charterholders achieve better returns
I passed all three levels on my first attempts (fact)...so I am among the elite
The designation is globally recognised and the exams are rigorousAs a charterholder I am the most qualified to manage your money
Charterholders commit to a code of ethicsEnrolling guarantees you will value bonds better
Facts and labelled opinions are fine; any link between the charter and superior results is not.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate48/63
Case: VII(B)

Chintu's LinkedIn headline

Chintu passes Level I and is enrolled for Level II. He changes his LinkedIn headline to "Chintu | CFA Level I" and adds "CFA charter expected 2028".

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VII(B), twice. "CFA Level I" implies a partial designation, which does not exist. An expected charter date is not allowed because the award depends on passing Level III, work experience and Board approval. Correct: "Passed Level I of the CFA Program" or "Level II candidate in the CFA Program".

No partial designations and no expected dates; state the level passed or the level you are a candidate for.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate49/63
Case: VII(B)

First attempt, three times

Sharma ji's firm drafts two ads. Ad 1: "All our partners are CFA charterholders who passed each level at the first attempt." (True.) Ad 2 adds: "...which is why our funds beat the market every year."

Verdict (tap)

Ad 1: no violation. Passing in consecutive attempts is a fact and may be stated. Ad 2: violation of VII(B). It links the charter and first-attempt passes to superior investment performance, implying charterholders achieve better results.

A true fact about passing is fine; tying it to returns is an exaggeration.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate50/63
Case: VII(B)

The lapsed charterholder's cards

Ravi earned his charter, then quit work for two years of travel. He stopped paying dues and stopped filing the Professional Conduct Statement, so his membership lapsed. Back home as a freelance analyst, he prints cards reading "Ravi Iyer, CFA" without reinstating his membership.

Verdict (tap)

Violation of VII(B). Without active membership he has lost the right to use the designation, so the cards misrepresent his status. He may say he was a charterholder in the past, or reinstate his membership and then use it again.

A lapsed member may not use CFA after his name until membership is reinstated.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate51/63
Exam trap

VII(B) traps examiners love

  • "Passed in three consecutive attempts" is a fact: allowed. Linking it to skill or returns is not.
  • "CFA, Level II" or "CFA candidate, expected 2028": both violations.
  • A charterholder who stops paying dues or filing the PCS loses the right to use CFA, even if retired, unless reclassified as retired.
  • Opinions such as "the charter helped my career" are allowed when framed as opinion.
  • Someone who passed but is not enrolled for the next exam is not a current candidate; say "passed Level I".
Read every reference to CFA literally: is it true, current, and free of performance claims?
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate52/63
Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. VI(A): avoid conflicts if reasonable; else disclose to employer, clients and prospects, prominently and plainly.
  2. Family holdings count. Footnotes are not prominent.
  3. VI(B): clients, then employer, then you. Front-running is the classic breach.
  4. Family client accounts: equal treatment, not first, not last.
  5. Hot IPOs: abstain or pre-clear. Blackouts and pre-clearance stop front-running.
  6. VI(C): disclose referral benefits paid or received, before the deal, with nature and value.
  7. VII(A): never reveal questions or topics tested or not tested; opinions are fine.
  8. VII(B): no partial CFA, no expected date, no performance claims; dues and PCS yearly.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the chapter summary.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate53/63
Exam question 1 of 10

Kavya, a CFA charterholder, owns 5,000 shares of a company she rates a buy. Her report discloses the holding in a footnote in 6-point type on page 31. Kavya most likely:

  1. A. complied with the Standards, because she disclosed the holding
  2. B. violated Standard VI(A), because the disclosure was not prominent
  3. C. violated Standard VI(B), because she owns a stock she recommends
Show answer

Answer: B. VI(A) requires disclosures to be prominent and in plain language, and a tiny footnote deep in the report is neither. A is wrong because disclosure that nobody can find does not count. C is wrong because owning a stock you recommend is not banned by VI(B); VI(B) is about trading ahead of clients.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate54/63
Exam question 2 of 10

A portfolio manager who is a CFA charterholder manages her parents' fee-paying account at her firm. For hot IPOs she fills every other suitable client first and gives her parents whatever is left. She most likely:

  1. A. violated Standard VI(B) by disadvantaging a client account
  2. B. complied with the Standards, because clients come before family
  3. C. violated only Standard VI(A), by not disclosing the family relationship
Show answer

Answer: A. Family accounts that are client accounts must be treated like any other client account, neither favoured nor disadvantaged, so putting them last breaches VI(B). B is wrong because her parents are clients too. C is wrong because the problem is unequal allocation, not a missing disclosure.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate55/63
Exam question 3 of 10

  2. B. disclose the estimated value of the benefit
  3. C. obtain the client's written consent before paying a referral fee
Show answer

Answer: C. VI(C) requires disclosure, before any formal agreement, of the nature and estimated value of referral benefits. It does not require the client's written consent. A and B are both required parts of the disclosure, so they are not the least likely.

Pick an answer before you tap.

Ch 7: Standards VI and VII: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a Member or Candidate58/63
Exam question 6 of 10

Pinky, a trader who is neither a CFA Institute member nor a candidate, buys shares for herself just before executing a large client buy order in the same stock. Has Pinky violated the CFA Institute Standards?

Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)1/44
Before you start

The cast, and words this chapter uses

A Mumbai investment firm. Sharma ji trusts nothing without data ("Data dikhao"); Pinky is sure of everything, especially when wrong.

  • CFA Institute: runs the CFA Program and owns and administers the GIPS standards.
  • Portfolio: investments managed for one client, or for many investors together in a fund.
  • Prospective client: someone the firm is trying to win as a client.
  • Benchmark: an index a manager is compared with, such as the Nifty 50.
  • Gross / net of fees: return before / after the manager's fee.
You can start this chapter cold. Everything it needs is on this card.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)2/44
Story

The brochure with one fund in it

A pension trust in Pune is choosing a manager. Pinky's firm sends a glossy brochure: one fund, one year, +31%. It does not mention the firm's 14 other portfolios, the two it closed after bad years, or that the 31% is before fees.

Every number in the brochure may be true and the picture is still false. The Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) exist to stop this: they are ethical standards for calculating and presenting investment performance, built on fair representation and full disclosure.

True numbers chosen selectively still mislead; GIPS fixes how performance is calculated and shown.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)3/44
Problem 1 of 3

Cherry-picking: showing only the winners

Cherry-picking means presenting the best-performing portfolios, or the best time periods, as if they were typical.

  • Showing one "representative" account that happens to be the best one.
  • Choosing the start date that makes the record look best: since the March 2020 crash bottom, say.
  • Showing a model or back-tested portfolio instead of real client money.

GIPS answers with composites: every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio must sit in at least one composite, so the losers are counted too.

Cherry-picking hides the typical client's experience; composites force every eligible portfolio into the record.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)4/44
Problem 2 of 3

Survivorship bias: the graveyard nobody shows

Survivorship bias appears when portfolios or funds that were closed, usually after bad results, vanish from the record. Only the survivors are left, so the average looks better than what clients really got.

In the chart, the three survivors average 9.33%. Add back the two closed portfolios and the true average is 1.00%.

GIPS requires terminated portfolios to stay in a composite's history up to the last full period the firm managed them.

Dropping dead portfolios inflates returns; GIPS keeps terminated portfolios in the historical record.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)5/44
Problem 3 of 3

Inconsistent methods: apples versus mangoes

ChoiceHow firms differ without a standard
Return methodSome let client deposits inflate returns; some adjust for them
FeesGross versus net, often unlabelled
PeriodAny start date, any length
ValuationStale or generous prices for hard-to-value assets
Which accountsHand-picked versus all

Without one method, a 14% and an 11% cannot be compared. GIPS sets common calculation rules and required disclosures so the numbers line up.

GIPS makes performance comparable by fixing the method, the accounts included and the disclosures.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)6/44
What GIPS are

Ethical standards for performance, not a rulebook for returns

The GIPS standards are voluntary, ethical standards for calculating and presenting investment performance, based on fair representation and full disclosure.

Stated objectives include: promote investor interests and confidence; ensure accurate and consistent data; win worldwide acceptance of a single standard; promote fair global competition among firms; and promote industry self-regulation.

They do not say what return is "good". They make sure the return you see is honestly built. 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms

GIPS are about honest, comparable presentation of performance, not about achieving any level of return.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)7/44
Who benefits

Investors, firms and the industry

WhoBenefit
Investors and prospectsComplete, fairly presented records; firms compared like for like; more confidence
FirmsA "global passport": a small Mumbai firm competes for a London mandate on equal terms; credibility; tighter internal controls
Asset ownersShow their oversight boards they follow global best practice
IndustrySelf-regulation, fewer misleading claims, fair global competition
Investors gain comparability and trust; firms gain a global passport; the industry gains self-regulation.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)8/44
Who runs GIPS

CFA Institute owns them, the world helps

CFA Institute owns the GIPS standards (GIPS is its registered trademark) and creates and administers them together with the GIPS standards governing bodies. Local GIPS Standards Sponsors, such as CFA Society India, promote them in their markets.

History: in 1995 CFA Institute (then AIMR) funded a committee to build a global standard from the AIMR Performance Presentation Standards. The first GIPS appeared in 1999. The current edition is the 2020 edition, effective 1 January 2020. 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms

CFA Institute sponsors and administers GIPS; the current edition is the 2020 GIPS standards.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)9/44
Voluntary, then binding

Nobody forces you; once you claim, you comply fully

Compliance is voluntary. GIPS are an industry standard, not a law, and firms choose to adopt them. The push usually comes from clients, consultants and competition for mandates.

But once a firm claims compliance, it must meet all applicable requirements, including CFA Institute's Guidance Statements, interpretations and Q&As, and notify CFA Institute when it first claims and every year after.

If a law conflicts with GIPS, the firm follows the law and discloses the conflict. Regulators are encouraged to act against false claims of compliance.

GIPS compliance is voluntary; a claim of compliance is a promise to meet every applicable requirement.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)10/44
Who can claim

Firms and asset owners, never people or products

Only an organisation that manages assets can claim GIPS compliance:

  • Investment firms that manage money for clients follow the GIPS Standards for Firms.
  • Asset owners (pension funds, endowments, foundations) can also claim, under their own GIPS provisions.

A person cannot be "GIPS compliant", nor can a single fund, composite or product. Software and consultants who do not manage the assets cannot claim compliance either; they can only help a firm comply or ask managers to comply.

Claims of compliance belong to firms (and asset owners), never to individuals or single products.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)11/44
Firm-wide

Compliance is all or nothing, firm-wide

GIPS must be applied on a firm-wide basis. Compliance cannot be met for one composite, one pooled fund or one portfolio.

The firm must be defined as an investment firm, subsidiary or division held out to the public as a distinct business entity. Signs of a distinct business entity: it is a separate legal entity, it serves a distinct market or client type, or it uses its own investment process.

The firm definition sets the boundary for total firm assets and for what must comply. It must be disclosed in every GIPS Report.

Define the firm first; then everything inside that boundary must comply.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)12/44
No partial claims

No "except for", no "calculated in accordance with"

A firm that does not meet all applicable requirements must not say it complies "except for...", or make any statement that suggests compliance or partial compliance.

Statements that a calculation method is "in accordance with", "in compliance with" or "consistent with" GIPS are also prohibited.

To make a first claim, the firm needs at least 5 years of compliant history (or since inception if younger), then adds a year at a time until it shows at least 10 years.

There is no half-compliant firm: meet every applicable requirement or make no GIPS claim.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)13/44
Decision path

May this organisation claim GIPS compliance?

Three gates, in order:

  1. Is the claimant an organisation that manages assets (a firm or an asset owner), not a person, a product or software?
  2. Is the firm defined, and is every part of it inside the compliance programme?
  3. Are all applicable requirements met, including guidance statements and Q&As?

Three yeses: claim compliance with the required wording. Any no: make no claim and no hint of one.

A claim needs the right claimant, firm-wide coverage and every requirement met.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)14/44
Fundamentals 1

Composites: the anti-cherry-picking box

A composite is a group of one or more portfolios managed to a similar investment mandate, objective or strategy. Its return is the asset-weighted average of its portfolios' returns.

The core rule: every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio must be included in at least one composite. (The 2020 text says this of segregated accounts; pooled funds join any composite whose definition they meet.)

Firms must create composites for every strategy they offer as a segregated account. Terminated portfolios stay in the history. Portfolios cannot be shifted between composites to flatter results.

Every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio goes into at least one composite, so the record shows what clients really got.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)15/44
Fundamentals 2

Actual, fee-paying, discretionary: three filters

FilterMeaningFails if
ActualReal moneyModel, simulated or back-tested
Fee-payingThe firm earns a feeFree account (may be included, not required)
DiscretionaryFirm can follow its strategyClient limits block the strategy

The firm writes its own definition of discretion and applies it consistently. A client who bans all bank stocks from a banking-heavy strategy may make the account non-discretionary. Non-discretionary portfolios must not be included in composites.

All three filters passed means the portfolio must be in a composite; non-discretionary ones are kept out.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)16/44
Worked example

Composite return versus the brochure

Ganga Asset Managers runs three discretionary, fee-paying large-cap accounts all year: A (Rs 200 crore, +10%), B (Rs 100 crore, +4%), C (Rs 50 crore, -2%). The marketing team wants to show only A. What is the composite return (beginning-of-year asset weights)?

  1. Total assets = 200 + 100 + 50 = Rs 350 crore
  2. Weighted sum = 200 x 10 + 100 x 4 + 50 x (-2) = 2,000 + 400 - 100 = 2,300
  3. Composite return = 2,300 / 350 = 6.57%
Composite return = 6.57%, not the 10% of account A. All three accounts must be in the composite.
The composite return is asset-weighted across all qualifying portfolios, which is why cherry-picked figures look better.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)17/44
Fundamentals 3

Pooled funds

A pooled fund is a fund whose ownership interests may be held by more than one investor: mutual funds, hedge funds, private equity funds. A segregated account is owned by a single client.

Under the 2020 edition:

  • A pooled fund must be included in any composite whose definition it meets.
  • Firms must make every reasonable effort to give a GIPS Pooled Fund Report to prospective investors in limited distribution pooled funds (funds not sold to the general public).
Pooled funds have many owners; they join matching composites and get their own GIPS Pooled Fund Reports.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)18/44
Fundamentals 4

Time-weighted return: judge the manager, not the client

Clients, not managers, decide when money comes in or goes out. A return that rises because a client happened to deposit before a rally says nothing about skill.

The time-weighted return (TWR) removes the effect of these external cash flows: measure the return between cash flows, then link the sub-period returns geometrically.

GIPS requires TWR in most cases, with portfolios valued at least monthly and on the date of every large cash flow. A money-weighted return is allowed only when the firm controls the cash flows and the fund is, for example, closed-end, fixed-life or illiquid (typical of private equity).

TWR strips out client cash flows so the return reflects the manager's decisions.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)19/44
Worked example

TWR versus money-weighted, one bad deposit

A client puts Rs 100 lakh in. Period 1: it grows to 110 (+10%). The client then adds Rs 100 lakh, so 210 is invested. Period 2: it falls to 189 (-10%). What is the time-weighted return over both periods?

  1. Sub-period returns: R1 = 110/100 - 1 = +10%; R2 = 189/210 - 1 = -10%
  2. TWR = (1 + 0.10) x (1 - 0.10) - 1 = 1.10 x 0.90 - 1 = -1.00%
  3. For contrast, the money-weighted return (IRR of -100, -100, +189) is about -3.71% per period: more money was invested in the bad period
TWR = -1.00% over the two periods. The manager is judged on this, not on the client's unlucky timing.
TWR ignores how much money was invested when; the money-weighted return does not, which is why GIPS usually requires TWR.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)20/44
Fundamentals 5

GIPS Reports: what prospects receive

A GIPS Report is either a GIPS Composite Report or a GIPS Pooled Fund Report.

  • The firm must make every reasonable effort to give a GIPS Composite Report to all prospective clients when they first become prospects. It may not pick and choose who gets one.
  • Prospects who are still prospects get an updated report at least every 12 months.
  • Reports show at least 5 years of annual returns (building to 10), a benchmark, and required disclosures such as the firm definition and the compliance statement.
Every prospect gets the GIPS Report for the relevant composite, with returns, benchmark and disclosures, updated yearly.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)21/44
Fundamentals 6

The compliance statement: exact words only

Once a firm meets all requirements, it must disclose its compliance using the prescribed compliance statement. It begins: "[Firm] claims compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS®) and has prepared and presented this report in compliance with the GIPS standards."

  • Not verified: it adds that the firm has not been independently verified.
  • Verified: it names the verified periods and adds a paragraph explaining what verification covers.

No part may be left out; changes may only add words. A separate line says GIPS is a CFA Institute trademark and CFA Institute does not endorse the firm. 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms

Use the exact compliance statement for the firm's verification status; never trim it.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)22/44
Verification

Verification: an outside check of the whole firm

Verification is a process in which an independent third-party verifier tests a firm on a firm-wide basis.

It gives assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures for composite and pooled fund maintenance, and for the calculation, presentation and distribution of performance, have been designed in compliance with GIPS and implemented firm-wide.

It is optional but strongly recommended and considered best practice. A firm can claim compliance without it, as long as its statement says it has not been verified.

Verification is optional, independent and firm-wide; it tests policies and procedures, not one track record.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)23/44
Verification limits

What verification does not do

VerificationPerformance examination
ScopeWhole firmOne composite or pooled fund
TestsPolicies and proceduresThat fund or composite's performance
Required?No, strongly recommendedNo, optional extra
Certifies a return?NoGives extra assurance on that report

The verified-firm statement itself says verification does not give assurance on the accuracy of any specific performance report.

Verification does not certify a composite's numbers; a separate performance examination is needed for that.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)24/44
Exam trap

GIPS traps examiners love

  • Voluntary: GIPS are an industry standard that firms choose to adopt, not a law.
  • Only firms (and asset owners) claim compliance, firm-wide. Not people, not one composite, not software.
  • No partial compliance, no "except for", no "calculated in accordance with GIPS".
  • Verification is optional, done by an independent third party, and covers the whole firm.
  • Verification does not certify any composite's returns.
  • Every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio must be in at least one composite.
Firm-wide, all-or-nothing, voluntary, verification optional: four phrases that answer most GIPS questions.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)25/44
Case: claim of compliance

"Our flagship fund is GIPS compliant"

Pinky's firm brings its Rocket Fund up to GIPS rules for calculation and presentation. The rest of the firm's portfolios are not. Its new ad says: "Rocket Fund: a GIPS-compliant fund."

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect claim. Compliance can only be claimed by a firm, on a firm-wide basis. It cannot be met for a single pooled fund, composite or portfolio, so a "GIPS-compliant fund" claim is not allowed.

A single product can never be GIPS compliant on its own.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)26/44
Case: claim of compliance

Chintu's CV line

Chintu helped his firm build its composites and now calls himself a "GIPS-compliant analyst" on his CV and LinkedIn. His firm does claim GIPS compliance and has been verified.

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect claim. Individuals cannot be GIPS compliant; only firms (and asset owners) can claim compliance. Chintu may factually say that he worked on his firm's GIPS compliance, for example "helped maintain composites for a GIPS-compliant firm".

People do GIPS work; only firms claim GIPS compliance.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)27/44
Case: claim of compliance

Compliant, except for one thing

Ganga Asset Managers meets every GIPS requirement except the valuation frequency for its real estate portfolios. Its pitch book says: "We comply with the GIPS standards except for the valuation of our real estate portfolios."

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect claim. A firm that does not meet all applicable requirements may not claim compliance "except for" anything, or say anything that implies partial compliance. It must fix the gap first, then claim compliance in full.

"Except for" is not allowed in a GIPS claim.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)28/44
Case: claim of compliance

Returns "calculated per GIPS"

Pinky's firm does not claim GIPS compliance, but it does use time-weighted returns. Its factsheet footnote says: "Returns calculated in accordance with the GIPS standards."

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect claim. Statements that a calculation method is "in accordance with", "in compliance with" or "consistent with" GIPS are prohibited. A non-compliant firm may describe its method in plain words, such as "time-weighted returns, net of fees", without mentioning GIPS.

Using a GIPS-style method does not let a firm borrow the GIPS name.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)29/44
Case: claim of compliance

The verified firm, done right

Sharma Capital defines itself as the whole asset management company, puts every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio into composites, meets all requirements and has a verifier test the whole firm. Its GIPS Composite Reports carry the full two-paragraph verified-firm compliance statement and go to every prospective client.

Verdict (tap)

Correct claim. It is a firm, compliance is firm-wide, all requirements are met, the exact statement is used without omissions, and reports go to all prospects. Verification was optional, and the firm chose it.

Right claimant, firm-wide, every requirement, exact statement: that is a valid claim.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)30/44
Case: claim of compliance

"Our 18% has been verified"

A firm has a firm-wide GIPS verification but no performance examination. Its ad says: "Our Growth composite returned 18% last year, and this figure has been verified by an independent firm."

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect claim. Verification tests firm-wide policies and procedures; it does not provide assurance on any specific composite's performance. Only a separate performance examination of that composite would add assurance on its numbers.

Verification is about the firm's processes, not a stamp on one composite's return.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)31/44
Case: claim of compliance

The two portfolios that vanished

Two clients left Pinky's firm in 2025 after heavy losses. Her firm claims GIPS compliance, but when it updates its composite history it removes both accounts' past returns, "because they are not clients any more".

Verdict (tap)

Incorrect. Terminated portfolios must stay in the composite's historical performance up to the last full period the firm managed them. Removing them creates survivorship bias, so the firm's claim of compliance would be false.

Closed portfolios stay in composite history; deleting them breaks GIPS.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)32/44
Exam trap

III(D) and GIPS are not the same thing

Standard III(D) Performance Presentation binds every CFA Institute member and candidate: performance they present must be fair, accurate and complete.

GIPS is voluntary and applies to firms. A member whose firm is not GIPS compliant does not violate III(D) for that reason alone, but must still present performance fairly.

For members showing the record of assets they manage, the Standards of Practice Handbook calls GIPS compliance the best method to meet III(D), and members should encourage their firms to comply.

Not complying with GIPS is not itself a violation; misleading performance presentation is.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)33/44
Sharma ji's red pen

8 things to remember

  1. GIPS: voluntary ethical standards for presenting performance; fair representation, full disclosure.
  2. They fight cherry-picking, survivorship bias and inconsistent methods.
  3. CFA Institute owns and administers GIPS; current edition: 2020.
  4. Only firms (and asset owners) claim compliance, firm-wide. Never a person, fund or software.
  5. No partial claims: no "except for", no "calculated in accordance with GIPS".
  6. Every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio is in a composite; terminated ones stay in history.
  7. TWR removes client cash flows. Prospects get a GIPS Report with the exact compliance statement.
  8. Verification: optional, independent, firm-wide; it does not certify any composite's return.
Scribbled by Sharma ji on the chapter summary.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)34/44
Exam question 1 of 10

Which of the following is most likely a problem the GIPS standards were created to address?

  1. A. Firms presenting only their best-performing portfolios as representative
  2. B. Firms charging fees that are too high for retail clients
  3. C. Firms taking too much risk relative to their benchmarks
Show answer

Answer: A. GIPS target how performance is calculated and presented; composites stop cherry-picking. B is wrong because GIPS do not set fee levels, only require fees to be disclosed and returns labelled gross or net. C is wrong because GIPS do not limit risk taking.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)35/44
Exam question 2 of 10

Compliance with the GIPS standards is best described as:

  1. A. mandatory for all CFA charterholders' employers
  2. B. voluntary, but once claimed all applicable requirements must be met
  3. C. voluntary, and a firm may choose which requirements to follow
Show answer

Answer: B. Compliance is voluntary, but a firm that claims it must meet all applicable requirements. A is wrong because no CFA Institute rule forces an employer to comply. C is wrong because partial compliance is not allowed.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)36/44
Exam question 3 of 10

Which entity can most likely claim compliance with the GIPS standards?

  1. A. A portfolio manager who calculates her own track record using GIPS methods
  2. B. A mutual fund whose returns are calculated using GIPS methods
  3. C. An investment management firm that applies the standards firm-wide
Show answer

Answer: C. Only firms (and asset owners) can claim compliance, and only on a firm-wide basis. A is wrong because individuals cannot claim compliance. B is wrong because compliance cannot be met for a single pooled fund or composite.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)37/44
Exam question 4 of 10

A firm meets every GIPS requirement except one disclosure. Which statement may it make?

  1. A. "We comply with GIPS except for one disclosure."
  2. B. No statement claiming or implying compliance with GIPS
  3. C. "Our returns are calculated in accordance with GIPS."
Show answer

Answer: B. A firm that does not meet all requirements must not claim compliance or imply partial compliance. A is a prohibited "except for" claim. C is prohibited because statements that calculations are "in accordance with" GIPS are not allowed.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)38/44
Exam question 5 of 10

Under GIPS, which portfolios must be included in at least one composite?

  1. A. All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios
  2. B. Only portfolios that have outperformed their benchmark
  3. C. All portfolios, including non-discretionary and model portfolios
Show answer

Answer: A. Every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio must be in at least one composite. B is wrong because selecting winners is the cherry-picking GIPS forbids. C is wrong because non-discretionary portfolios must not be included and model portfolios are not actual.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)39/44
Exam question 6 of 10

A firm's composite contains three portfolios at the start of the year: Rs 300 crore returning 8%, Rs 100 crore returning 2% and Rs 100 crore returning -4%. Using beginning asset weights, the composite return is closest to:

  1. A. 2.0%
  2. B. 4.4%
  3. C. 8.0%
Show answer

Answer: B. Asset-weighted: (300 x 8 + 100 x 2 + 100 x (-4)) / 500 = (2,400 + 200 - 400) / 500 = 2,200 / 500 = 4.4%. A is the simple equal-weighted average of the three returns, which ignores asset size. C is the best portfolio alone: cherry-picking.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)40/44
Exam question 7 of 10

GIPS generally require time-weighted returns because they:

  1. A. remove the effect of external cash flows controlled by the client
  2. B. always produce higher returns than money-weighted returns
  3. C. include the effect of the timing of client deposits
Show answer

Answer: A. TWR strips out client-driven cash flows so the return reflects the manager's decisions. B is wrong because TWR can be higher or lower than a money-weighted return. C describes a money-weighted return, not a TWR.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)41/44
Exam question 8 of 10

Which statement about GIPS verification is most accurate?

  1. A. It is required before a firm may claim compliance
  2. B. It certifies the accuracy of each composite's performance
  3. C. It tests, firm-wide, whether policies and procedures comply with GIPS
Show answer

Answer: C. Verification is an independent, firm-wide test of whether the firm's policies and procedures are designed in compliance and implemented firm-wide. A is wrong because verification is optional (strongly recommended). B is wrong because verification does not provide assurance on any specific performance report; a performance examination adds that for one composite.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)42/44
Exam question 9 of 10

A GIPS-compliant firm removes a portfolio that was terminated after large losses from its composite's past returns. The firm's action is:

  1. A. acceptable, because only current clients belong in composites
  2. B. not consistent with GIPS, because terminated portfolios stay in historical composite performance
  3. C. acceptable if the firm has been verified
Show answer

Answer: B. Terminated portfolios must remain in the composite's history up to the last full period they were managed; removing them creates survivorship bias. A is wrong because composites include past portfolios for the periods they were managed. C is wrong because verification does not permit breaking a requirement.

Pick an answer before you tap.
Ch 8: Introduction to the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)43/44
Exam question 10 of 10

Which party is least likely to benefit directly from the GIPS standards?

  1. A. A prospective client comparing two managers
  2. B. A firm competing for mandates in another country
  3. C. A firm that wants to show only its best accounts to prospects
Show answer

Answer: C. GIPS stop selective presentation, so a firm that wants to show only its best accounts is the party whose practice they block. A benefits from comparable, complete records. B benefits from GIPS acting as a global passport.
